# Overview



DARUMA-binding is a machine-learning tool that identifies **binding sites within intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs)** of proteins. IDRs are stretches of a protein that do not fold into a rigid 3D structure — yet many of them carry out important work by *binding* to other molecules. Instead of predicting a whole-protein structure, DARUMA-binding works at the **residue level**: for every amino acid in your input sequence, it answers the question *"how likely is this single amino acid to participate in binding?"*

This page gives you a beginner-friendly map of the entire repository: what the tool produces, how the pieces fit together architecturally, the two ways to run it, and where the datasets live. No prior knowledge of deep learning is assumed — deeper technical pages are linked at the end.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L3), [caid/DARUMA-binding/README.md](caid/DARUMA-binding/README.md#L1-L8)

## What DARUMA-binding Predicts

You provide a **FASTA file** (the standard text format for amino acid sequences, e.g. `>protein1 / MEKVYQ...`), containing one or more sequences. For each sequence, DARUMA-binding writes an output file with eight pieces of per-residue information:

| # | Output field | What it means for a beginner |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Accession / FASTA header | The name of the protein you submitted |
| 2 | Amino acid sequence | The sequence itself, echoed back |
| 3 | Binding probability | A number between 0 and 1 per residue — higher means more likely to bind |
| 4 | Binary binding prediction | The probability converted to `1` (binding) or `0` (non-binding) using a fixed **threshold of 0.26** |
| 5 | Predicted pLDDT | A per-residue confidence-like structural score (a concept borrowed from AlphaFold) |
| 6 | Predicted RSA | Relative solvent accessibility — how "exposed" each residue is |
| 7 | Predicted SS3 | Three-state secondary structure: `H` (helix), `S` (strand), `C` (coil) |
| 8 | Predicted SS8 | A finer, eight-state secondary structure classification |

Fields 5–8 are "bonus" structural predictions that the model computes internally as intermediate features — they are included in the output so you can inspect them. The full output format is documented step-by-step in [Output Format Reference](3-output-format-reference).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L26-L53)

## How It Works at a Glance

Internally, DARUMA-binding is a small ensemble of **1-D convolutional neural networks** operating on protein language model embeddings. The big picture:

1. **Featurization** — Each input sequence is converted into per-residue vectors using **ProtT5** (`Rostlab/prot_t5_xl_half_uniref50-enc`), a pre-trained protein language model. Every amino acid becomes a 1024-dimensional numeric vector.
2. **Auxiliary feature extraction** — Three frozen ("DAF") sub-networks predict pLDDT, RSA, and 8-state secondary structure from those embeddings, compressing them into a compact **12-feature-per-residue** structural fingerprint.
3. **Binding head** — A **multi-kernel convolutional module** scans that fingerprint at six different window sizes (kernels of width 3, 7, 15, 31, 63, and 127 residues) and produces a final two-class score per residue: binding vs. non-binding.
4. **Decision** — The score becomes a probability via softmax; probabilities ≥ **0.26** are labeled as binding residues.
5. **Output** — A result writer records everything into your output file, one line per residue.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["FASTA input<br/>(one or more sequences)"] --> B["ProtT5 Featurizer<br/>per-residue embeddings, L × 1024"]
    B --> C["Auxiliary DAF heads (frozen)<br/>DAF-pLDDT · DAF-RSA · DAF-SS8"]
    C --> D["Structural fingerprint<br/>12 features per residue"]
    D --> E["Multi-kernel conv binding head<br/>kernels 3/7/15/31/63/127 → 48 channels → 2 classes"]
    E --> F["Softmax → binding probability<br/>threshold = 0.26 → 1/0 label"]
    F --> G["Output file<br/>8 fields per residue"]
```

The command-line entry point `src/daruma_binding/predict.py` wires these stages together: it reads the FASTA, builds the featurizer on your chosen device (CPU or GPU), loads the trained weights (`daruma_binding_weight.pth`), runs each sequence, and streams results to disk.

Sources: [src/daruma_binding/predict.py](src/daruma_binding/predict.py#L54-L71), [src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L136-L187), [caid/DARUMA-binding/README.md](caid/DARUMA-binding/README.md#L10-L25), [README.md](README.md#L29-L30)

> [!TIP]
> The auxiliary DAF heads run under `torch.no_grad()` inside the binding head — they are treated as a fixed, pre-trained feature extractor, not as trainable parts of the final model. This is why their predictions can safely be exported as extra outputs.

## Two Ways to Run DARUMA-binding

The same predictive core is packaged in **two delivery modes**, aimed at different audiences:

| Aspect | Native CLI (`src/`) | CAID 4 Docker (`caid/`) |
|---|---|---|
| Who it's for | Developers running predictions locally | CAID 4 benchmark participants |
| Input | FASTA file only — ProtT5 embedding is generated automatically inside the pipeline | FASTA file **plus** a precomputed ProtT5 embedding (NumPy `.npy`, shape `L × 1024`) |
| Command style | `python src/daruma_binding/predict.py -i input.fasta -o output.txt -d cpu` | `docker run` with `--fasta`, `--embeddings`, `--output`, `--device` flags |
| Output format | Full 8-field per-residue report | Compact CAID format: `position · residue · probability · binary` |
| Sample assets | `examples/example.fasta` + `examples/predict_example.sh` | `caid/DARUMA-binding/sample_data/` (DP03914 fasta + npy + expected caid output) |

The native mode is the recommended starting point for beginners because the language model embedding step is handled for you. Docker mode exists specifically because the CAID community experiment requires standardized, containerized submissions with embeddings supplied externally.

Sources: [src/daruma_binding/predict.py](src/daruma_binding/predict.py#L31-L36), [examples/README.md](examples/README.md#L3-L7), [examples/predict_example.sh](examples/predict_example.sh#L1-L4), [caid/DARUMA-binding/README.md](caid/DARUMA-binding/README.md#L10-L41), [caid/DARUMA-binding/README.md](caid/DARUMA-binding/README.md#L44-L52)

## Repository Map

The repository is organized into five top-level areas, each with a distinct role:

```
DARUMA-binding/
├── src/daruma_binding/      ← Core prediction package
│   ├── predict.py           ← CLI entry point
│   └── backend/             ← Model definitions + trained weights (.pth)
├── examples/                ← Minimal runnable example (fasta + shell script)
├── caid/DARUMA-binding/     ← CAID 4 Docker submission (self-contained copy)
├── data/                    ← Validation & test datasets (training data lives on Zenodo)
├── reproduction/            ← Scripts that regenerate the paper's figures & tables
├── requirements.txt         ← Python dependencies (PyTorch installed separately)
├── LICENSE
└── README.md
```

| Directory | Purpose | Key contents |
|---|---|---|
| `src/daruma_binding/` | Inference source code | `predict.py` CLI, `backend/models.py` (architecture), `backend/model_weights/daruma_binding_weight.pth` (trained weights), `backend/functions.py` (FASTA reading, featurizing, result writing) |
| `examples/` | Your first run | `example.fasta`, `predict_example.sh` |
| `data/` | Evaluation datasets | `training/`, `validation/`, `test/` subfolders |
| `reproduction/` | Paper reproducibility | `scripts/figure_2.py` … `figure_4.py`, `table_1.py` … plus processed `results/caid2/`, `results/caid3/`, `results/occlusion_analysis/` |
| `caid/DARUMA-binding/` | Docker image source | `Dockerfile`, `run_example_docker.sh`, `sample_data/` |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L67-L74), [src/daruma_binding/predict.py](src/daruma_binding/predict.py#L27-L28), [examples/README.md](examples/README.md#L1-L13), [data/README.md](data/README.md#L3-L31), [reproduction/README.md](reproduction/README.md#L1-L2)

## Datasets and Benchmarks at a Glance

The data story splits into two tiers — everything needed to *evaluate* the model is in this repository, while the large *training* corpus is archived externally:

- **Training data** (`data/training/train_binding.txt` plus companion files for the DAF models): the full-scale training corpora are hosted on **Zenodo** (DOI `10.5281/zenodo.24127965`), keeping the repository lightweight.
- **Validation data** (`data/validation/`): paired `val_binding.txt`, `val_plddt.txt`, `val_rsa.txt`, `val_ss.txt` files used during model development.
- **Test data** (`data/test/`): three blind benchmark sequence sets obtained from the CAID Web Portal — **CAID 2 Binding**, **CAID 3 Binding**, and **CAID 3 Binding-IDR**.
- **Processed results** (`reproduction/results/`): ready-made prediction outputs (`caid2_DARUMA-binding.caid`, `caid3_DARUMA-binding.caid`, per-protein occlusion CSVs) so you can regenerate every figure and table of the paper without re-running inference.

The archived manuscript version itself is also on Zenodo (DOI `10.5281/zenodo.24133355`), and a hosted **web server** implementation is available at `https://antepontem.org/daruma_binding/` if you want to try predictions without installing anything.

Sources: [data/README.md](data/README.md#L9-L31), [README.md](README.md#L57-L62), [README.md](README.md#L77-L93), [get_repo_structure: reproduction/results](reproduction/results)

## Environment and Installation Requirements

DARUMA-binding is a Python 3 tool with a deliberately minimal dependency set — the only heavy requirement is **PyTorch, which you must install separately** so it matches your operating system, GPU, and CUDA version. After that, `pip install -r requirements.txt` pulls in NumPy, HuggingFace Transformers, SentencePiece, scikit-learn, SciPy, and Matplotlib. The environment officially validated by the authors is:

| Component | Version |
|---|---|
| OS | Ubuntu 18.04.5 LTS |
| Python | 3.10.19 |
| PyTorch | 1.12.1+cu102 |
| CUDA | 10.2 |
| transformers (ProtT5) | 4.30.2 |
| numpy | 1.26.4 |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L10-L24), [README.md](README.md#L96-L101), [requirements.txt](requirements.txt#L1-L7)

4. **[Prediction Pipeline Architecture](5-prediction-pipeline-architecture)** — then descend into the architecture: the convolutional backbone ([FEU and PU](6-convolutional-backbone-feu-and-pu)), the [auxiliary structural feature heads](7-auxiliary-structural-feature-heads), and the [multi-kernel binding head](8-multi-kernel-conv-binding-head).
5. **[ProtT5 Embedding Chunking Strategy](9-prott5-embedding-chunking-strategy)** and **[Inference Orchestration and Decision Threshold](10-inference-orchestration-and-decision-threshold)** — how long sequences are handled and how the 0.26 cutoff is applied.
6. Finally, the evaluation side: [CAID Benchmark Datasets](11-caid-benchmark-datasets), [Training Data and Zenodo Archive](12-training-data-and-zenodo-archive), [Reproducing Paper Figures and Tables](13-reproducing-paper-figures-and-tables), [Evaluation Metrics: AUC, APS, Fmax](14-evaluation-metrics-auc-aps-fmax), and [Occlusion-Based Feature Attribution](15-occlusion-based-feature-attribution).

If you want to see the tool without any local setup at all, the public web server (`https://antepontem.org/daruma_binding/`) offers the same predictions through a browser.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L26-L41), [README.md](README.md#L85-L88), [examples/predict_example.sh](examples/predict_example.sh#L1-L4)

> [!TIP]
> The trained weights ship *inside* the repository (`backend/model_weights/daruma_binding_weight.pth`) — you don't download anything extra to run inference. Only the large training corpora require the Zenodo archive, which keeps the clone-and-run experience fast.

# Quick Start



This page gets you from a fresh clone to your first binding-site prediction in four steps: install dependencies, verify what ships in the box, run the bundled example, and inspect the output. It covers only the **local installation path** — Docker-based execution is covered in [Docker and CAID Usage](4-docker-and-caid-usage), and the detailed per-line output schema is documented in [Output Format Reference](3-output-format-reference).

DARUMA-binding predicts, for **each residue** in a protein sequence, whether it is likely to be a **binding site within an intrinsically disordered region (IDR)**. You feed it a FASTA file; it writes a plain-text report with binding probabilities, binary calls (threshold `0.26`), and auxiliary predicted structural features (pLDDT, RSA, SS3, SS8).

## Step 0 — What Happens When You Run It

Before typing any commands, it helps to know what the pipeline does end-to-end. The diagram below is the complete runtime flow of `predict.py`: no external servers, no manual feature engineering — everything from embedding to writing results happens in one command.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["FASTA input<br/>(1..N sequences)"] --> B["read_fasta<br/>normalize residues<br/>(UBJOZ → X)"]
    B --> C["ProtT5 encoder<br/>Rostlab/prot_t5_xl_half_uniref50"]
    C --> D["DARUMA-binding model<br/>(bundled .pth weights)"]
    D --> E["ResultWriter<br/>8-line record per sequence"]
    E --> F["output.txt"]
```

Two facts from this flow matter for your first run: the DARUMA model weights are **bundled inside the repository** (`backend/model_weights/daruma_binding_weight.pth`), but the ProtT5 encoder is fetched **from the Hugging Face Hub on first run** — so your machine needs internet access the first time only.

Sources: [predict.py](src/daruma_binding/predict.py#L54-L73), [functions.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/functions.py#L26-L56), [README.md](README.md#L60-L66)

## Step 1 — Install Dependencies

Clone the repository and install the Python dependencies. The critical detail: **PyTorch is installed separately** because the correct build depends on your operating system and CUDA environment — the `requirements.txt` intentionally does not pin it.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/antepontem/DARUMA-binding.git
cd DARUMA-binding
# 1. Install PyTorch for your OS/CUDA from pytorch.org
# 2. Then install the rest:
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

The declared dependencies and the environment the authors actually tested on are summarized below:

| Dependency | Pinned Version | Role in This Tool |
|---|---|---|
| numpy | 1.26.4 | Numerical array handling |
| transformers | 4.30.2 | ProtT5 tokenizer + encoder (`T5Tokenizer`, `T5EncoderModel`) |
| sentencepiece | 0.2.1 | Tokenizer backend required by T5 |
| scikit-learn | 1.7.2 | Metric utilities |
| scipy | 1.15.3 | Scientific computing |
| matplotlib | 3.10.8 | Plotting utilities |

| Tested Environment Component | Value |
|---|---|
| OS | Ubuntu 18.04.5 LTS |
| Python | 3.10.19 |
| PyTorch | 1.12.1+cu102 |
| CUDA | 10.2 |

If your CUDA/OS combination differs from the tested environment, install the matching PyTorch build for your hardware; the code itself adapts at runtime (see device selection in Step 3).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L5-L20), [requirements.txt](requirements.txt#L1-L7), [README.md](README.md#L94-L103)

## Step 2 — Verify What Ships in the Box

After cloning, your working tree contains exactly what you need to run inference — nothing to download or compile manually. The layout relevant to Quick Start is:

```
DARUMA-binding/
├── requirements.txt                  # installable dependencies
├── src/daruma_binding/
│   ├── predict.py                    # ← the CLI entry point
│   └── backend/
│       ├── functions.py              # FASTA parsing, ProtT5 embedder, result writer
│       ├── models.py                 # model definition
│       └── model_weights/
│           └── daruma_binding_weight.pth   # ← trained weights, bundled
├── examples/
│   ├── example.fasta                 # ← ready-made input (3 human proteins)
│   └── predict_example.sh            # one-line example launcher
└── data/                             # benchmark datasets (not needed to run)
```

> [!TIP]
> **First-run network requirement**: the DARUMA weights load locally from `backend/model_weights/`, but `T5Tokenizer.from_pretrained("Rostlab/prot_t5_xl_half_uniref50-enc")` and `T5EncoderModel.from_pretrained(...)` download the ~1.2B-parameter half-precision ProtT5 encoder from the Hugging Face Hub the first time you run. It is cached locally afterwards, so subsequent runs work offline.

The `examples/` directory is your fastest path: `example.fasta` contains three well-known human IDP proteins — p53 (P04637), 4EBP1 (Q13541), and CREB1 (P16220) — each in standard multi-line FASTA format.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L60-L66), [functions.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/functions.py#L44-L51), [example.fasta](examples/example.fasta#L1-L9)

## Step 3 — Run Your First Prediction

The single entry point for inference is `src/daruma_binding/predict.py`. Run the bundled example:

```bash
cd examples
bash predict_example.sh
```

This executes `python3 ../src/daruma_binding/predict.py -i example.fasta -o example.out`. Note the script uses a **relative path** (`../src/...`), so it must be launched from inside the `examples/` directory. For arbitrary inputs, call the script directly from the repository root:

```bash
python src/daruma_binding/predict.py -i your_sequences.fasta -o results.txt
```

The complete CLI contract is small — three flags, one of them with default behavior worth understanding:

| Flag | Long Form | Required | Default | Behavior |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `-i` | `--input` | No* | — | Path to input FASTA file |
| `-o` | `--output` | **Yes** | — | Path where predictions are written |
| `-d` | `--device` | No | `0` | `"cpu"` for CPU, or GPU index `0`, `1`, ... |

*\*Although `-i` is not marked `required=True` in the argument parser, the script fails immediately without it when `read_fasta` attempts to open the file.*

**Device selection logic** (worth reading before your first GPU run): if you pass `-d cpu`, prediction runs on CPU. If you pass a GPU index (or accept the default `0`) and CUDA is available, that GPU is used. If CUDA is **not** available, the script silently falls back to CPU — it will still work, just slower:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["argparse: -d device"] --> B{"d == 'cpu'?"}
    B -- Yes --> C["torch.device('cpu')"]
    B -- No --> D{"CUDA available?"}
    D -- Yes --> E["cuda.set_device(d)<br/>torch.device(f'cuda:{d}')"]
    D -- No --> C
    C --> F["print using device"]
    E --> F
```

What happens next is a per-sequence loop: each FASTA record is embedded with ProtT5, passed through the DARUMA-binding model, and written to disk. Processing continues across all sequences in the file — with `example.fasta`, expect three "Processing ..." progress lines before completion.

> [!TIP]
> **Silent CPU fallback is a feature and a trap**: if your PyTorch build lacks CUDA (e.g., you installed the CPU-only wheel), `-d 0` does **not** error — it quietly runs on CPU. If your run seems unusually slow, check the printed `Using <device> device.` line at startup to confirm where the work is happening.

Sources: [predict_example.sh](examples/predict_example.sh#L1-L4), [examples/README.md](examples/README.md#L1-L13), [predict.py](src/daruma_binding/predict.py#L31-L51), [predict.py](src/daruma_binding/predict.py#L66-L71)

## Step 4 — Verify the Output

Open `examples/example.out`. It is plain text, self-documenting: the file begins with a comment block describing its layout, followed by an 8-line record per input sequence. Here is the schema at a glance:

| Line | Content | Format |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Accession / FASTA header | after `>` prefix |
| 2 | Amino acid sequence | single line, concatenated |
| 3 | Binding probability per residue | comma-separated floats, 4 decimals |
| 4 | Binary binding call per residue | comma-separated `1`/`0`, threshold = **0.26** |
| 5 | Predicted pLDDT per residue | comma-separated floats |
| 6 | Predicted relative solvent accessibility (RSA) | comma-separated floats |
| 7 | Three-state secondary structure (SS3) | `H` helix / `S` strand / `C` coil |
| 8 | Eight-state secondary structure (SS8) | `H, G, I, E, B, T, S, -` |

The header comments are written programmatically by `ResultWriter` at file creation, so every output file carries its own legend — you never need to memorize the schema. For the full field-by-field interpretation guide (including what the SS8 letters mean and how to parse the files), continue to [Output Format Reference](3-output-format-reference).

Sources: [functions.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/functions.py#L136-L158), [README.md](README.md#L45-L58)

## Input Requirements

Your only obligation as a user is a valid FASTA file — one or more sequences, headers beginning with `>`. Three parsing behaviors are worth knowing upfront:

| Concern | Behavior | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Multiple sequences | Supported | All records in the file are processed sequentially |
| Sequence line breaks | Handled | Newlines and spaces within a sequence are stripped |
| Non-standard residues (`U`, `B`, `J`, `O`, `Z`) | Remapped to `X` | Applied at both parsing and embedding stages |
| Sequence length | No practical limit | ProtT5 embedding automatically chunks at 2048 residues with 512 overlap |

The last row means you can submit very long proteins without splitting them yourself — the chunking is internal to the embedder.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L39-L43), [functions.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/functions.py#L12-L23), [functions.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/functions.py#L61-L62)

## Troubleshooting

These are the failure modes a first-time runner is most likely to hit, mapped to causes and fixes:

| Symptom | Likely Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `ModuleNotFoundError: torch` | PyTorch not installed separately | Install PyTorch for your OS/CUDA **before** `pip install -r requirements.txt` |
| `ModuleNotFoundError: sentencepiece` | `requirements.txt` not installed | Run `pip install -r requirements.txt` |
| Run hangs at start on first execution | ProtT5 encoder downloading from Hugging Face | Expected on first run (~GB download); ensure network access. Later runs use the local cache |
| `FileNotFoundError` on `-i` path | Input path does not exist, or `-i` omitted | Verify the path; note `-o` is the only flag the parser marks required, so a missing `-i` surfaces as a file error, not an argparse error |
| Prediction unexpectedly slow | CUDA unavailable → silent CPU fallback | Check the `Using ... device.` startup line; install a CUDA-enabled PyTorch build or pass `-d cpu` explicitly |
| `bash predict_example.sh` fails from repo root | Script uses relative path `../src/...` | Run it from inside the `examples/` directory, or call `predict.py` directly with paths relative to your current directory |

Sources: [predict.py](src/daruma_binding/predict.py#L31-L51), [functions.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/functions.py#L44-L51), [predict_example.sh](examples/predict_example.sh#L1-L4)

## No Installation? Try the Web Server

If you only need a quick prediction without setting up an environment, DARUMA-binding is also hosted as a web server at **https://antepontem.org/daruma_binding/**. The local installation described on this page is for batch processing, automation, and reproducibility.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L88-L92)

# Output Format Reference



This page is the complete field manual for the file that DARUMA-binding writes when you run a prediction: what each line means, how values are formatted, and how to parse the result back into your own scripts. It covers the **native output format** produced by `src/daruma_binding/predict.py`, the multi-sequence file layout, and the separate CAID benchmark format that appears in the Docker submission code. Everything here is derived directly from the writing code, so you can treat this page as ground truth for building parsers.

Sources: [predict.py](src/daruma_binding/predict.py#L15-L16), [README.md](README.md#L45-L58)

## The Output Pipeline: From FASTA to Result File

Understanding where the output file comes from makes its structure predictable. When you run `predict.py`, your FASTA file passes through four stages, and the final stage is the one that decides the file format. The header lines are written once when the file is created; each input sequence then appends one fixed 8-line block. This means the output size is always deterministic: **8 header lines + 8 lines per input sequence**.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["input.fasta<br/>(1..N sequences)"] --> B["read_fasta()<br/>header → accession<br/>UBJOZ → X"]
    B --> C["SequenceFeaturizer<br/>ProtT5 embeddings"]
    C --> D["model.predict_from_seq()<br/>result dict with 9 keys"]
    D --> E["ResultWriter.append_write()<br/>8 lines per sequence"]
    F["ResultWriter.__init__<br/>8 header comment lines"] --> E
    E --> G["output file<br/>8 header + 8N lines"]
```

The prediction loop is deliberately simple: for every accession in the input dictionary, `predict_from_seq(seq)` returns a result dictionary, and `result_writer.append_write()` immediately flushes it to disk. There is no batching or post-hoc file rewriting — each sequence is appended in input order.

Sources: [predict.py](src/daruma_binding/predict.py#L63-L71), [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L245-L257)

## File Anatomy: Header Block and Per-Sequence Blocks

The writer is implemented in the `ResultWriter` class. Its constructor opens the output path in write mode and stamps **eight comment lines** (each starting with `#`) that act as a built-in legend describing the eight lines that follow for every sequence. Its `append_write` method then appends exactly eight lines per sequence. Both blocks are shown in the table below.

| Position | Content | Format | Written by |
|---|---|---|---|
| Header 1–8 | Self-describing legend (one `#` line per data line type) | Plain text, `#` prefix | `ResultWriter.__init__` |
| Block line 1 | Accession / FASTA header | `>{accession}` | `append_write` |
| Block line 2 | Amino acid sequence | Raw one-letter codes, no separators | `append_write` |
| Block line 3 | Binding probability per residue | Comma-separated, 4 decimal places | `append_write` |
| Block line 4 | Binary binding prediction | Comma-separated `1` / `0` | `append_write` |
| Block line 5 | Predicted pLDDT | Comma-separated, 4 decimal places | `append_write` |
| Block line 6 | Predicted RSA | Comma-separated, 4 decimal places | `append_write` |
| Block line 7 | SS3 secondary structure | Comma-separated letters `H`/`S`/`C` | `append_write` |
| Block line 8 | SS8 secondary structure | Comma-separated letters `H`/`G`/`I`/`E`/`B`/`T`/`S`/`-` | `append_write` |

> [!TIP]
> Because the 8-line block layout is fixed, any per-residue line (lines 3–8) must contain **exactly one value per residue** — split on `,` and you get a list whose length equals the sequence length on line 2. This invariant is the simplest sanity check for a parser.

Sources: [functions.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/functions.py#L136-L158), [README.md](README.md#L47-L58)

## Line-by-Line Field Reference

### Line 1 — Accession

The first line of each block repeats the FASTA header exactly as parsed, prefixed with `>`. The `read_fasta` parser takes the whole header line (everything up to the first newline) as the accession key, so a UniProt-style header like `sp|P04637|P53_HUMAN Cellular tumor antigen p53 ...` is preserved in full. If your input headers are long, expect long output headers — nothing is truncated or reformatted.

Sources: [functions.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/functions.py#L12-L23), [example.fasta](examples/example.fasta#L1-L8)

### Line 2 — Sequence

Line 2 is the sequence actually used for prediction, not necessarily byte-identical to your input. The reader concatenates wrapped FASTA lines (removing newlines and spaces) and rewrites the ambiguous/non-standard residues `U`, `B`, `J`, `O`, `Z` as `X` before prediction. The same `X`-substitution is applied again inside the embedding step, so line 2 always reflects the model-facing sequence.

Sources: [functions.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/functions.py#L12-L23), [functions.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/functions.py#L61-L62)

### Line 3 — Binding Probability

Each residue's binding probability is written as a float with **exactly 4 decimal places** (Python's `{x:.4f}` format), comma-separated. Values are produced by applying softmax over the model's two output classes and taking the binding-class probability, so every value lies in `[0.0, 1.0]`.

Sources: [functions.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/functions.py#L153), [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L77-L79)

### Line 4 — Binary Binding Prediction

Line 4 is the discretized version of line 3: a residue is `1` (binding) if its probability is **strictly greater than 0.26**, and `0` (non-binding) otherwise. The code applies `(prob > self.threshold).astype(int)`, and the threshold itself is stored on the model as `0.26`, chosen to maximize the F1 score on validation data. The exact value is also echoed in the header legend, so parsers never need to hard-code it.

| Probability value | Line 3 text | Line 4 text | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.2599 | `0.2599` | `0` | Below threshold → non-binding |
| 0.2600 | `0.2600` | `0` | Equal to threshold → non-binding (strict `>`) |
| 0.2601 | `0.2601` | `1` | Above threshold → binding |

> [!TIP]
> The comparison is **strictly greater than** (`>`), so a probability of exactly 0.26 rounds down to non-binding. When filtering segments by line 4, remember that line 4 is a rounded view of line 3: a value printed as `0.2600` could be anything in `[0.26000, 0.26005)` — always re-derive decisions from line 3 if exactness matters.

Sources: [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L198), [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L228-L229), [functions.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/functions.py#L143)

### Line 5 — pLDDT

Predicted pLDDT (per-residue structural confidence) is written with 4 decimal places, but note the scale: the model stores it as a probability and multiplies it by 100 before returning, so **pLDDT values range from 0 to 100**, not 0 to 1. A value like `57.3920` means moderate confidence; values near 90+ indicate high model confidence in that residue's structural position.

Sources: [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L232), [functions.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/functions.py#L155)

### Line 6 — RSA

Predicted relative solvent accessibility is written with 4 decimal places and **stays on the probability scale (0 to 1)** — unlike pLDDT, it is not rescaled. Together, lines 5 and 6 expose the auxiliary structural features the model computes internally from dedicated pLDDT and RSA heads, which is why the README describes them as "predicted structural features used by the model."

Sources: [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L233), [README.md](README.md#L53-L58)

### Lines 7–8 — SS3 and SS8 Secondary Structure

The final two lines give secondary structure as one character per residue, comma-separated. SS3 uses the `q3_to_char` mapping, and SS8 uses `q8_to_char` applied to the argmax of the model's 8-way structure head. The SS3 prediction is not a separate model output: helix, sheet, and coil are derived by summing the corresponding groups of SS8 probabilities and taking the argmax.

| SS3 letter | Meaning | SS8 letter | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `H` | Helix | `H` | Alpha helix |
| `S` | Sheet / strand | `G` | 3-10 helix |
| `C` | Coil | `I` | pi helix |
| | | `E` | Extended strand |
| | | `B` | Isolated beta bridge |
| | | `T` | Turn |
| | | `S` | Bend |
| | | `-` | Other (coil) |

Sources: [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L205-L220), [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L234-L238), [functions.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/functions.py#L146-L147)

## Worked Example (Schematic)

The repository ships a three-sequence example input (`example.fasta`, containing human p53, 4EBP1, and CREB1) and a shell script that produces the output file `example.out`. The output file itself is generated when you run the script, so it is not committed — the block below is a schematic (truncated, values illustrative) showing exactly how one sequence block looks on disk:

```text
# Line1. accession
# Line2. sequence
# Line3. binding probability (float)
# Line4. binding prediction (1:binding, 0:non-binding), threshold=0.26
# Line5. pLDDT (float)
# Line6. RSA (float)
# Line7. SS3 (H:Helix, S:Strand, C:Coil)
# Line8. SS8 (H:Alpha helix, G:3-10 helix, I:pi helix, E:Extended strand, B:Isolated beta bridge, T:Turn, S:Bend, -:Other (coil))
>sp|P04637|P53_HUMAN Cellular tumor antigen p53 OS=Homo sapiens OX=9606 GN=TP53 PE=1 SV=4
MEEPQSDPSVEPPLSQETF...
0.0123,0.0098,0.0105,...
0,0,0,...
34.2211,35.0098,33.8875,...
0.3312,0.3098,0.2905,...
C,C,C,...
-,C,C,...
```

Read each block as an aligned column view of the same residues: position *i* of the sequence corresponds to position *i* in every comma-separated list below it. The seven lines after `>` are strictly parallel — same length, same residue order.

Sources: [examples/README.md](examples/README.md#L3-L13), [predict_example.sh](examples/predict_example.sh#L1-L4), [example.fasta](examples/example.fasta#L1-L8)

## Multi-Sequence Output and Parsing Tips

Input files may contain any number of sequences, and all of them land in one output file in input order. A three-sequence FASTA like `example.fasta` therefore produces 8 header lines followed by 24 data lines. Because the header legend is written only once at file creation, downstream parsers should skip `#` lines and treat every `>` line as the start of a new block. The following beginner-friendly snippet recovers all eight fields per sequence:

```python
blocks = {}
with open("example.out") as f:
    for raw in f:
        line = raw.rstrip("\n")
        if line.startswith("#"):
            continue                      # header legend (appears once)
        if line.startswith(">"):
            accession = line[1:]          # new block begins
            blocks[accession] = []
        else:
            blocks[accession].append(line)

for ac, lines in blocks.items():
    seq    = lines[1]                                        # raw sequence
    prob   = [float(v) for v in lines[2].split(",")]         # binding probability
    binary = [int(v)   for v in lines[3].split(",")]         # 1/0 binding
    plddt  = [float(v) for v in lines[4].split(",")]         # 0–100 scale
    rsa    = [float(v) for v in lines[5].split(",")]         # 0–1 scale
    ss3    = lines[6].split(",")                             # H/S/C per residue
    ss8    = lines[7].split(",")                             # H/G/I/E/B/T/S/- per residue
```

| Gotcha | Detail |
|---|---|
| Line 2 has no commas | Only lines 3–8 are comma-separated; `split(",")` on line 2 would give garbage |
| pLDDT vs RSA scales | pLDDT is ×100 (0–100), RSA is a raw probability (0–1) |
| Threshold is strict `>` | 0.2600 exactly → `0`; re-derive from line 3 if precision matters |
| Sequence was normalized | `UBJOZ` → `X` and line-joining mean line 2 may differ from your raw input |
| Header legend appears once | 8 `#` lines total regardless of sequence count, not per block |

Sources: [predict.py](src/daruma_binding/predict.py#L66-L71), [functions.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/functions.py#L149-L158)

## DARUMA Native Format vs. CAID Format

Do not confuse the native format above with the **CAID benchmark format**, which is produced only by the CAID 4 submission code in `caid/DARUMA-binding/` (run through Docker with precomputed embeddings). That format emits one line *per residue* with tab-separated columns, as verified in the sample result `DP03914.caid`:

```text
>DP3914
1	M	0.331179	1
2	Q	0.335192	1
```

| Dimension | Native format (`predict.py`) | CAID format (`caid/` Docker) |
|---|---|---|
| Layout | 8 lines per sequence (residue values inline) | L lines per sequence (one row per residue) |
| Columns per residue | Probability, binary, pLDDT, RSA, SS3, SS8 as lists | Position, residue, probability, binary |
| Delimiter | Commas (probability/binary/pLDDT/RSA), commas (SS letters) | Whitespace / tabs |
| Extra structural outputs | pLDDT, RSA, SS3, SS8 included | Not included |
| Header legend | 8 `#` comment lines at top | None |
| Input requirement | FASTA only (embeddings computed internally) | FASTA + precomputed ProtT5 `.npy` embedding |

Sources: [caid/DARUMA-binding/README.md](caid/DARUMA-binding/README.md#L44-L52), [DP03914.caid](caid/DARUMA-binding/sample_data/DP03914.caid#L1-L6)

One related format warning: the files in `data/training/train_binding.txt` look superficially similar (header, sequence, labels) but are **training labels**, not predictions — their binary lines are plain `0`/`1` strings without commas or probability values. Use them as benchmark/training references only.

Sources: [train_binding.txt](data/training/train_binding.txt#L1-L3)

## What to Read Next

To go deeper from here, the catalog offers a natural progression. For the alternate output path (Docker + CAID format, embedding precomputation), continue to [Docker and CAID Usage](4-docker-and-caid-usage). To understand *why* the output contains pLDDT, RSA, and SS8 — the auxiliary heads that produce those fields — see [Prediction Pipeline Architecture](5-prediction-pipeline-architecture) and [Auxiliary Structural Feature Heads](7-auxiliary-structural-feature-heads). For the reasoning behind the 0.26 threshold you saw on line 4, read [Inference Orchestration and Decision Threshold](10-inference-orchestration-and-decision-threshold). If you want to compare your own outputs against benchmark results, [CAID Benchmark Datasets](11-caid-benchmark-datasets) explains the evaluation files.


# Docker and CAID Usage



This page covers the self-contained Docker packaging of DARUMA-binding that was submitted to the CAID 4 experiment, found in the `caid/` directory. You will learn what the Docker image contains, how to run a prediction inside the container, how to interpret the CAID-format output file, and how this minimal environment differs from the full repository pipeline. All commands shown here are verified against the repository's scripts and source code.

## Why a Dedicated CAID Docker Image

CAID (Critical Assessment of protein Intrinsic Disorder prediction) is a community-wide benchmarking experiment in which participating groups submit a fixed, reproducible version of their predictor. The root README explicitly identifies the `caid/` directory as "Code submitted to CAID 4", and notes that this code originally lived in the repository root before being relocated [README.md](README.md#L60-L66), [README.md](README.md#L84-L86).

Because experiment evaluators must rerun your method exactly as submitted, the CAID packaging follows a minimal-and-frozen philosophy: the image bundles only the inference code, the trained weights, and two pinned dependencies (`numpy==1.26.4`, `torch==2.2.2`) [requirements.txt](caid/DARUMA-binding/requirements.txt#L1-L2). Everything needed to turn an embedding into a prediction lives inside the image; everything expensive or external (the ProtT5 language model itself) stays outside. The project README is explicit that "ProtT5 model and weights: not included in this Docker image" — the container consumes **precomputed** embeddings only [README.md](caid/DARUMA-binding/README.md#L19-L31).

The diagram below shows how the pieces fit together at runtime: your data files enter through a volume mount, the container's entrypoint processes them using its baked-in weights, and the output is written back into the mounted directory.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Host["Your machine (host)"]
        SD["sample_data/<br/>DP03914.fasta + DP03914.npy"]
        OUT["DP03914.caid<br/>(written back to host)"]
    end
    subgraph Image["daruma-binding:v0.1.0 image"]
        EP["ENTRYPOINT<br/>python3 daruma_binding/predict.py"]
        M["models.py + utils.py<br/>(inference code)"]
        W["backend/model_weights/<br/>daruma_binding_weight.pth"]
    end
    SD -- "volume mount<br/>$PWD/sample_data → /work" --> EP
    EP --> M
    M --> W
    EP -- "writes /work/DP03914.caid" --> OUT
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L60-L66), [requirements.txt](caid/DARUMA-binding/requirements.txt#L1-L2), [README.md](caid/DARUMA-binding/README.md#L19-L31)

## Inside the Image: The Dockerfile Walkthrough

The Dockerfile is only 20 lines, and each line makes a deliberate packaging decision worth understanding before you run anything.

The image starts from `python:3.10-slim`, a lightweight official Python base rather than a GPU-capable or heavyweight image [Dockerfile](caid/DARUMA-binding/Dockerfile#L1-L3). It then installs exactly the two pinned requirements before copying any code — this ordering takes advantage of Docker's layer caching, so dependency installation is skipped on rebuilds when only source files change [Dockerfile](caid/DARUMA-binding/Dockerfile#L5-L6).

Four `COPY` instructions assemble the application: the `daruma_binding/` package (which includes the model weights at `backend/model_weights/daruma_binding_weight.pth`), the `sample_data/` example files, the local run script, and documentation/license files [Dockerfile](caid/DARUMA-binding/Dockerfile#L8-L12). Because the weights are copied in, **no model download is needed at runtime** — the image is fully self-sufficient for inference.

The environment variables pin CPU threading behavior inside the container: OpenMP and MKL at 8 threads, OpenBLAS and NumExpr at 1 [Dockerfile](caid/DARUMA-binding/Dockerfile#L14-L17). This mirrors the settings applied programmatically in `predict.py` itself [predict.py](caid/DARUMA-binding/daruma_binding/predict.py#L26-L37), so the thread configuration holds whether the code runs inside Docker or directly on a host.

The final two lines define the container's behavior as a command-line tool. `ENTRYPOINT ["python3", "daruma_binding/predict.py"]` means the Python script *is* the container — any arguments you place after the image name in `docker run` are appended to this script's command line. The default `CMD ["--help"]` means running the bare image with no arguments prints the script's usage help [Dockerfile](caid/DARUMA-binding/Dockerfile#L19-L20).

| Directive | What it does | Why it matters for you |
|---|---|---|
| `FROM python:3.10-slim` | Minimal Python 3.10 base | Small image; no GPU stack preinstalled |
| `RUN pip install -r requirements.txt` | Installs numpy + torch only | Reproducible, frozen dependency set |
| `COPY daruma_binding /app/daruma_binding` | Code **and** model weights | No runtime weight download needed |
| `COPY sample_data /app/sample_data` | Bundled example files | Image works out of the box |
| `ENV OMP/MKL/OPENBLAS/NUMEXPR...` | Pins threading | Deterministic CPU resource usage |
| `ENTRYPOINT ["python3", "daruma_binding/predict.py"]` | Script = container | Args after image name go to `predict.py` |
| `CMD ["--help"]` | Default arguments | Bare `docker run` shows usage help |

Sources: [Dockerfile](caid/DARUMA-binding/Dockerfile#L1-L20), [predict.py](caid/DARUMA-binding/daruma_binding/predict.py#L26-L37)

> [!TIP]
> The `ENTRYPOINT`/`CMD` combination means `docker run daruma-binding:v0.1.0` with no arguments simply prints `predict.py`'s argparse help text — that is not an error, it is the container's designed default behavior.

## Running a Prediction with Docker, Step by Step

The canonical invocation is captured in `run_example_docker.sh`, which predicts binding residues for one example protein end-to-end [run_example_docker.sh](caid/DARUMA-binding/run_example_docker.sh#L1-L9):

```bash
docker run --rm \
  -v "$PWD/sample_data":/work \
  daruma-binding:v0.1.0 \
  --fasta /work/DP03914.fasta \
  --embeddings /work/DP03914.npy \
  --output /work/DP03914.caid \
  --device cpu
```

Each flag plays a specific role. `--rm` removes the container after it exits, since the only artifact you care about is the output file. The `-v "$PWD/sample_data":/work` mount makes your local `sample_data/` folder visible inside the container at `/work` — this is essential, because the container cannot see host files otherwise, and because writing output to `/work` persists it on your host. Note the path convention: input and output paths (`--fasta`, `--embeddings`, `--output`) must be **container-internal** paths like `/work/...`, while the volume mount determines where they land on your machine. Run the script from within the `caid/DARUMA-binding/` directory so that `$PWD/sample_data` resolves correctly.

The project README also shows `docker pull daruma-binding:v0.1.0` as the way to obtain the image before running [README.md](caid/DARUMA-binding/README.md#L32-L42).

The following flowchart traces what happens inside the container after you execute that command, from argument parsing through output writing:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["docker run --rm -v ...<br/>daruma-binding:v0.1.0"] --> B["ENTRYPOINT: predict.py<br/>receives appended CLI args"]
    B --> C{"--fasta provided?"}
    C -- yes --> D["read_single_fasta<br/>→ accession + sequence"]
    C -- no --> E["sequence = '-' placeholders<br/>header = 'sequence'"]
    D --> F["np.load embeddings<br/>→ float32 tensor"]
    E --> F
    F --> G{"FASTA length ==<br/>embedding rows?"}
    G -- no --> X["ValueError: length mismatch"]
    G -- yes --> H["Pick device:<br/>cuda:N if available, else cpu"]
    H --> I["Load weights (CPU map)<br/>→ model.to(device), eval mode"]
    I --> J["Reshape to (1, 1024, L)<br/>→ predict_from_x"]
    J --> K["softmax → moving-average smooth<br/>(kernel 7) → threshold 0.26"]
    K --> L["Write CAID file:<br/>>accession + 4-column rows"]
```

The full CLI contract, as defined by argparse in `predict.py`, is summarized here [predict.py](caid/DARUMA-binding/daruma_binding/predict.py#L46-L52):

| Short flag | Long flag | Required | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `-f` | `--fasta` | No | Input FASTA file; supplies the sequence ID and residue letters. If omitted, a generic `>sequence` header and `-` placeholders are used |
| `-e` | `--embeddings` | Yes | Precomputed ProtT5 per-residue embedding in NumPy `.npy` format, shape `L × 1024` |
| `-o` | `--output` | Yes | Path for the CAID-format prediction output file |
| `-d` | `--device` | No (default `cpu`) | `cpu`, or a GPU index such as `0`, `1`, ... |

Two validation behaviors protect beginners from silent mistakes. First, `read_single_fasta` rejects files whose first line is not a `>` header [utils.py](caid/DARUMA-binding/daruma_binding/utils/utils.py#L3-L14). Second, the script raises a `ValueError` if the FASTA sequence length does not match the first dimension of the embedding array — the classic failure mode when a `.npy` and a `.fasta` get out of sync [predict.py](caid/DARUMA-binding/daruma_binding/predict.py#L76-L77).

Sources: [run_example_docker.sh](caid/DARUMA-binding/run_example_docker.sh#L1-L9), [README.md](caid/DARUMA-binding/README.md#L32-L42), [predict.py](caid/DARUMA-binding/daruma_binding/predict.py#L46-L77), [utils.py](caid/DARUMA-binding/daruma_binding/utils/utils.py#L3-L14)

## Understanding the CAID Output Format

The output file follows the CAID submission format: one header line with the sequence identifier, then one tab-separated row per residue [predict.py](caid/DARUMA-binding/daruma_binding/predict.py#L89-L103). The bundled example output for protein DP03914 (708 residues) shows the format in practice [DP03914.caid](caid/DARUMA-binding/sample_data/DP03914.caid#L1-L15):

```text
>DP3914
1	M	0.331179	1
2	Q	0.335192	1
3	A	0.341306	1
4	R	0.347953	1
...
```

| Column | Content | Example from sample | Rule |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Residue position (1-based) | `1` | Sequential index over the sequence |
| 2 | Amino acid letter | `M` | From the FASTA, or `-` if no FASTA was given |
| 3 | Binding probability | `0.331179` | Softmax class-1 probability, 6 decimal places |
| 4 | Binary prediction | `1` | `1` if probability > 0.26, else `0` |

Two details of column 4 deserve attention. The decision threshold is fixed at `0.26`, which the code documents as the value maximizing F1 score on validation data [models.py](caid/DARUMA-binding/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L189-L193). And before thresholding, raw network probabilities pass through a **moving-average smoother with kernel size 7** (replicate padding at the boundaries) inside `predict_from_x` [models.py](caid/DARUMA-binding/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L196-L204). The probabilities printed in column 3 are therefore already smoothed values, and the binary column is derived from those smoothed values — do not expect column 4 to equal "raw probability > 0.26" recomputed by hand.

The same format is described in the CAID README's output section [README.md](caid/DARUMA-binding/README.md#L44-L52). For a deeper treatment of output conventions across both the CAID image and the full pipeline, see [Output Format Reference](3-output-format-reference).

Sources: [DP03914.caid](caid/DARUMA-binding/sample_data/DP03914.caid#L1-L15), [predict.py](caid/DARUMA-binding/daruma_binding/predict.py#L89-L103), [models.py](caid/DARUMA-binding/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L189-L204), [README.md](caid/DARUMA-binding/README.md#L44-L52)

> [!TIP]
> The binary column (column 4) is computed from the *smoothed* probability, not the raw network output — the moving-average smoothing (kernel 7) happens inside `predict_from_x` before both the probability values and the threshold comparison are produced.

## Device Selection and Resource Behavior

The `--device`/`-d` flag has forgiving semantics designed for benchmark environments. Passing `cpu` (as the example does) always runs on CPU. Passing a GPU index such as `0` selects `cuda:0`, but **only if CUDA is actually available** — otherwise the code silently falls back to CPU rather than crashing, printing which device was chosen [predict.py](caid/DARUMA-binding/daruma_binding/predict.py#L61-L66). This makes the container safe to run on machines without GPUs while still exploiting them when present. Note that using a GPU from inside a container additionally requires NVIDIA drivers and the NVIDIA Container Toolkit on the host; the image itself ships a standard pip-installed PyTorch.

Threading is deliberately constrained for predictable resource usage: `predict.py` sets 8 OpenMP/MKL threads, 1 thread each for OpenBLAS and NumExpr, and calls `torch.set_num_threads(8)` with `set_num_interop_threads(1)` before any tensor work [predict.py](caid/DARUMA-binding/daruma_binding/predict.py#L26-L37). These are mirrored by the `ENV` directives baked into the image [Dockerfile](caid/DARUMA-binding/Dockerfile#L14-L17). For very long proteins, inference is performed on the whole sequence at once with no chunking in this CAID path — the tensor is simply reshaped to `(1, 1024, L)` and fed to the model [predict.py](caid/DARUMA-binding/daruma_binding/predict.py#L85-L87). For a discussion of when and why chunking matters, see [ProtT5 Embedding Chunking Strategy](9-prott5-embedding-chunking-strategy).

Sources: [predict.py](caid/DARUMA-binding/daruma_binding/predict.py#L26-L87), [Dockerfile](caid/DARUMA-binding/Dockerfile#L14-L17)

## CAID Image vs. the Full Repository Pipeline

The CAID image is intentionally a stripped-down sibling of the full predictor in `src/`. The root README documents the full pipeline's richer interface and output set, which includes predicted pLDDT, RSA, and secondary structure alongside binding predictions [README.md](README.md#L45-L58). This table summarizes the practical differences so you can pick the right tool for your task:

| Aspect | `caid/` Docker image | Full repository (`src/`) |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | Frozen CAID 4 benchmark submission | General research/production use |
| Input format | Precomputed `.npy` ProtT5 embeddings (required) + optional FASTA | FASTA only (`-i example.fasta`) |
| Proteins per run | Single protein | One or more sequences per file |
| Embedding source | User-supplied `.npy` file | Generated internally by the pipeline |
| Output columns | Probability + binary binding only | Binding + pLDDT + RSA + SS3 + SS8 |
| Dependencies | Pinned inside the image (numpy, torch) | User installs PyTorch per OS/CUDA [README.md](README.md#L14-L20) |
| Invocation | `docker run ... daruma-binding:v0.1.0 <args>` | `python3 src/daruma_binding/predict.py -i ... -o ...` |

The contrast in invocation style is visible in the repository's own example scripts: the full pipeline is run directly with `python3 ../src/daruma_binding/predict.py -i example.fasta -o example.out` [predict_example.sh](examples/predict_example.sh#L1-L4), while the CAID path wraps everything in the container as shown above. Note also that `run_example.sh` inside the CAID directory runs the same `predict.py` directly on the host — useful for testing the code without Docker, using identical arguments [run_example.sh](caid/DARUMA-binding/run_example.sh#L1-L13).

If your goal is to predict from raw FASTA files with full structural-feature output, start with [Quick Start](2-quick-start). If you need to generate the `L × 1024` `.npy` embeddings the CAID image expects, see [ProtT5 Embedding Chunking Strategy](9-prott5-embedding-chunking-strategy). For how the CAID datasets themselves are organized and evaluated, see [CAID Benchmark Datasets](11-caid-benchmark-datasets).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L14-L20), [README.md](README.md#L45-L58), [predict_example.sh](examples/predict_example.sh#L1-L4), [run_example.sh](caid/DARUMA-binding/run_example.sh#L1-L13)

## Troubleshooting Common Issues

Beginners hitting the Docker workflow most often trip on path mapping, input mismatch, or device expectations. Each symptom below maps to a verified cause in the code.

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `ValueError: Length of sequence (X) does not match the first dimension of ProtT5 vector (Y)` | FASTA and `.npy` describe different-length sequences | Regenerate the embedding for the exact FASTA you pass via `--fasta` [predict.py](caid/DARUMA-binding/daruma_binding/predict.py#L76-L77) |
| `ValueError: Invalid FASTA format` | File missing a `>` header on line 1 | Ensure the first line starts with `>` [utils.py](caid/DARUMA-binding/daruma_binding/utils/utils.py#L9-L10) |
| Output file does not appear on host | Output path pointed inside the container but outside the mounted volume | Always write outputs to `/work` (the mounted directory) |
| Header says `>sequence` instead of your protein ID | `--fasta` was not provided | Pass `-f/--fasta` to get the real accession [predict.py](caid/DARUMA-binding/daruma_binding/predict.py#L96-L100) |
| Prints "Using cpu device" though you passed `-d 0` | CUDA not available inside container; code falls back silently | Set up NVIDIA Container Toolkit on the host, or accept CPU [predict.py](caid/DARUMA-binding/daruma_binding/predict.py#L61-L66) |
| Bare `docker run daruma-binding:v0.1.0` just prints help text | Default `CMD ["--help"]` is active | Append your arguments after the image name [Dockerfile](caid/DARUMA-binding/Dockerfile#L19-L20) |
| Container can't find `/work/DP03914.fasta` | Script run from a directory where `$PWD/sample_data` doesn't exist | `cd caid/DARUMA-binding/` before running the script |

Sources: [predict.py](caid/DARUMA-binding/daruma_binding/predict.py#L61-L100), [utils.py](caid/DARUMA-binding/daruma_binding/utils/utils.py#L9-L10), [Dockerfile](caid/DARUMA-binding/Dockerfile#L19-L20)

## Where to Go Next

You now know how to run the CAID submission container and read its output. The logical next steps in this documentation depend on your goal: to understand what happens inside the model between the embedding input and the probability output, continue to [Prediction Pipeline Architecture](5-prediction-pipeline-architecture); to understand how the 0.26 decision threshold and output conventions were established, see [Inference Orchestration and Decision Threshold](10-inference-orchestration-and-decision-threshold); to learn how to produce the `L × 1024` embeddings this container consumes, read [ProtT5 Embedding Chunking Strategy](9-prott5-embedding-chunking-strategy); and for a broader review of conventions covered earlier in this guide, revisit [Output Format Reference](3-output-format-reference).


# Prediction Pipeline Architecture



This page dissects the end-to-end inference path of DARUMA-binding: how a raw FASTA file is transformed into per-residue binding probabilities and auxiliary structural annotations. We trace every tensor transformation from input parsing through ProtT5 featurization, the two-stage neural core, threshold-based binarization, and final serialization. This is the architectural "map" of the system — detailed internals of individual components are delegated to their dedicated pages in the Deep Dive section.

## The Pipeline at a Glance

The system is a linear, single-pass pipeline orchestrated by one script (`predict.py`) that delegates to three cooperating modules in `backend/`. There is no batching across sequences — each protein flows through the entire chain independently, making the architecture inherently streaming-friendly and memory-predictable.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["FASTA file<br/>(-i input.fasta)"] --> B["read_fasta<br/>parse + residue normalization"]
    B --> C["SequenceFeaturizer<br/>ProtT5 embedding, chunked"]
    C --> D["(L, 1024) per-residue<br/>embedding"]
    D --> E["daruma_binding wrapper<br/>weights + threshold 0.26"]
    E --> F["Stage A: AF feature extractor<br/>pLDDT / RSA / SS8 heads"]
    F --> G["(1, L, 12) structural<br/>feature vector"]
    G --> H["Stage B: Multi-kernel conv<br/>binding head"]
    H --> I["(1, L, 2) logits"]
    I --> J["softmax, threshold 0.26<br/>probabilities + binary mask"]
    J --> K["ResultWriter<br/>8-line record per protein"]
```

The following table traces tensor shape evolution at every stage boundary — this is the contract each module must honor:

| Pipeline Stage | Producer | Input Shape | Output Shape | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FASTA parsing | `read_fasta` | raw text | `dict[str, str]` | accession → sequence |
| Featurization | `ProtT5Embedder.embed` | string, length L | `(L, 1024)` | chunked, overlap 512 |
| Batch + channel permute | `predict_from_seq` | `(L, 1024)` | `(1, 1024, L)` | Conv1d layout |
| AF feature extraction | `af_daruma_like_ProtT5_features` | `(1, 1024, L)` | `(1, L, 12)` | 2+2+8 concatenated heads |
| Multi-kernel conv | `MultiKernelConv1d_withDropout` | `(1, 12, L)` | `(1, 48, L)` | 6 kernels × 8 channels |
| Binding head output | 1×1 Conv1d | `(1, 48, L)` | `(1, L, 2)` | transposed back |
| Decision | `logit_to_prob` + threshold | `(1, L, 2)` | `(L,)` probs, `(L,)` binary | class 1 = binding |

Sources: [predict.py](/src/daruma_binding/predict.py#L57-L73), [models.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L222-L257), [functions.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/functions.py#L60-L117)

## Module Interaction Map

Responsibility is cleanly separated across three backend modules and the CLI entry point. `predict.py` performs no tensor math itself — it is pure orchestration: device resolution, one-time construction of the featurizer/model/writer, and a per-sequence loop.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class PredictPy["predict.py (CLI entry)"]
    class SequenceFeaturizer
    class ProtT5Embedder
    class DarumaBinding["daruma_binding (facade)"]
    class AfMk1dConv["af_..._mk1dconv_relu (binding model)"]
    class AfFeatures["af_..._features (AF extractor)"]
    class ResultWriter

    PredictPy --> SequenceFeaturizer : constructs once
    PredictPy --> DarumaBinding : passes featurizer in
    PredictPy --> ResultWriter : binds threshold
    SequenceFeaturizer --> ProtT5Embedder : delegates featurize()
    DarumaBinding --> AfMk1dConv : owns .model
    AfMk1dConv --> AfFeatures : .af_feature_extractor
    DarumaBinding --> ProtT5Embedder : via featurizer in predict_from_seq
    PredictPy --> ResultWriter : append_write() per sequence
```

| Module | Responsibility | Key Exports |
|---|---|---|
| `predict.py` | CLI, device resolution, sequence loop | script entry |
| `functions.py` | I/O and featurization | `read_fasta`, `SequenceFeaturizer`, `ResultWriter`, `ProtT5Embedder` |
| `models.py` | Neural architecture + inference facade | `daruma_binding`, `af_daruma_like_ProtT5_features_mk1dconv_relu` |

The `daruma_binding` class is the critical facade: it binds the frozen model weights, the decision threshold, the (currently disabled) smoother, and the featurizer into a single callable unit with `predict_from_seq()` as its public API. This facade pattern means `predict.py` never touches model internals — a deliberate isolation that keeps the neural graph opaque to the orchestrator.

Sources: [predict.py](/src/daruma_binding/predict.py#L21-L65), [models.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L190-L203), [functions.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/functions.py#L123-L133)

## Stage 1: Ingestion and Device Resolution

Two normalization steps occur before any neural computation. First, `read_fasta` splits the file into blocks, strips whitespace/newlines from sequences, and remaps ambiguous or non-canonical residue codes (`U`, `B`, `J`, `O`, `Z`) to `X` so downstream tokenizers never encounter invalid symbols. Second, the CLI device argument is resolved: `cpu` selects CPU; a numeric index selects `cuda:N` via `torch.cuda.set_device` — with a silent fallback to CPU if CUDA is unavailable. Note the asymmetry: device selection happens in `predict.py`, but the model is loaded to CPU first and then transferred, which avoids GPU-anchored checkpoints entirely.

| `-d` Argument | CUDA Available | Effective Device |
|---|---|---|
| `cpu` | either | `cpu` |
| `0`, `1`, … | yes | `cuda:N` (`set_device` called) |
| `0`, `1`, … | no | `cpu` (fallback, no error) |

Sources: [functions.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/functions.py#L12-L23), [predict.py](/src/daruma_binding/predict.py#L42-L55), [models.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L192-L195)

## Stage 2: Sequence Featurization

The featurizer wraps a single HuggingFace encoder — `Rostlab/prot_t5_xl_half_uniref50-enc` — instantiated in half precision and moved to the resolved device (`float()` conversion on CPU, where fp16 is unsupported). The `SequenceFeaturizer` is intentionally thin: it exists solely to bind a feature-type string to an embedder instance, making future alternative featurizations a one-line extension point. Inside `embed()`, the sequence runs under `torch.inference_mode()` and is processed in windows of `chunk_size=2048` with `overlap=512`, producing per-residue 1024-dimensional embeddings that are concatenated into a single `(L, 1024)` tensor. A second residue remap (`U`, `Z`, `O`, `B` → `X`) guards the tokenizer input.

The chunk/overlap/trim mechanics — why 256 residues are trimmed from each interior chunk boundary and how positional artifacts are avoided — are documented in detail on the dedicated embedding page: [ProtT5 Embedding Chunking Strategy](9-prott5-embedding-chunking-strategy).

Sources: [functions.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/functions.py#L26-L59), [functions.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/functions.py#L62-L66), [functions.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/functions.py#L123-L133)

## Stage 3: The Two-Stage Neural Core

The binding model is architecturally a **composition, not a monolith**: a frozen feature extractor (Stage A) feeding a trainable prediction head (Stage B). This split is the single most important structural decision in the pipeline.

**Stage A — Auxiliary Feature (AF) extractor.** Three parallel `daruma_like` networks (each a Conv1d stack: FEU encoder + PU pooling unit) predict pLDDT (2-class), RSA (2-class), and SS8 (8-class) independently from the same `(1, 1024, L)` embedding input. Each head internally zero-pads 60 residues on both sides before its convolution stack, then softmaxes and concatenates — producing a `(1, L, 12)` structural feature vector with layout `[plddt, 1-plddt, 1-rsa, rsa, ss0…ss7]`. The internal FEU/PU design is covered in [Convolutional Backbone: FEU and PU](6-convolutional-backbone-feu-and-pu) and per-head specialization in [Auxiliary Structural Feature Heads](7-auxiliary-structural-feature-heads).

> [!TIP]
> The AF extractor runs under `torch.no_grad()` inside the binding model's forward pass, so predicted structure is a **fixed input** to Stage B — no gradients flow back into the structural heads during binding inference. However, `return_af_features=True` (the production configuration) stores a `detach().requires_grad_(True)` copy of the features, re-anchoring a gradient leaf on the feature tensor. This is the deliberate hook that later enables gradient-based attribution analysis ([Occlusion-Based Feature Attribution](15-occlusion-based-feature-attribution)).

**Stage B — Multi-kernel binding head.** The `(1, L, 12)` feature vector is transposed to channel-first `(1, 12, L)` and passed through six parallel 1D convolutions with kernels spanning `[3, 7, 15, 31, 63, 127]` — capturing binding-motif context from local to long-range — each contributing 8 channels, concatenated to `(1, 48, L)`. A single 1×1 convolution then projects to 2 logits per residue. The multi-scale kernel rationale is detailed in [Multi-Kernel Conv Binding Head](8-multi-kernel-conv-binding-head).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph StageA["Stage A: AF extractor (no_grad, frozen)"]
        E["(1, 1024, L)"] --> P["pLDDT head → 2 probs"]
        E --> R["RSA head → 2 probs"]
        E --> S["SS8 head → 8 probs"]
        P --> CAT["concat dim=2"]
        R --> CAT
        S --> CAT
    end
    CAT -->|"(1, L, 12)<br/>detach + requires_grad_"| T["transpose → (1, 12, L)"]
    T --> MK["6 parallel Conv1d<br/>k=3,7,15,31,63,127 → (1, 48, L)"]
    MK --> O["1×1 Conv1d → (1, L, 2)"]
```

Sources: [models.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L135-L151), [models.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L154-L186), [models.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L173-L186)

## Stage 4: Decision and Post-Processing

Logits map to probabilities via a single softmax restricted to index 1 (`logit_to_prob`), yielding the binding probability per residue. A moving-average smoother is applied, but the production configuration instantiates it with `kernel_size=1` — a deliberate no-op (the `kernel_size=7` variant exists in the code but is commented out), so raw head probabilities are what get serialized. Binarization is a hard comparison against the fixed threshold `0.26`, chosen to maximize F1 on validation data. The selection methodology, sensitivity of this constant, and orchestration-level behavior around it belong to [Inference Orchestration and Decision Threshold](10-inference-orchestration-and-decision-threshold).

> [!TIP]
> The smoother's no-op is not dead code — `MovingAverageSmoothing(kernel_size=1)` still executes the full pad/unfold/mean path, returning the input unchanged. This preserves a single insertion point if smoothing is ever re-enabled, without changing the output contract of `predict_from_x`.

Sources: [models.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L76-L78), [models.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L222-L229), [models.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L197-L199)

## Stage 5: Result Assembly and Serialization

`predict_from_seq` closes the loop by un-stacking the `(L, 12)` AF matrix into human-interpretable channels: `plddt` (column 0, scaled ×100 to the 0–100 confidence scale), `rsa` (column 3), `ss8` (columns 4–12), and a derived SS3 where helix = Σ(ss0–ss2), strand = Σ(ss3–ss4), coil = Σ(ss5–ss7). Discrete SS strings are produced by argmax through the `q8_to_char` / `q3_to_char` maps, and the original sequence is re-attached — yielding a flat result dictionary that is the sole interface between the neural world and I/O.

`ResultWriter` was opened once at startup (writing the 8-line format header) and appends one record per sequence — stream-friendly for multi-protein FASTA inputs:

| Output Line | Content | Source Field |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `>accession` | FASTA header |
| 2 | sequence | input sequence |
| 3 | binding probability, 4-decimal floats | `prob` |
| 4 | binary prediction (1/0) | threshold 0.26 comparison |
| 5 | pLDDT (float) | AF column 0 × 100 |
| 6 | RSA (float) | AF column 3 |
| 7 | SS3 string (H/S/C) | derived argmax |
| 8 | SS8 string (H/G/I/E/B/T/S/-) | derived argmax |

The byte-level format specification lives in [Output Format Reference](3-output-format-reference).

Sources: [models.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L205-L220), [models.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L245-L257), [functions.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/functions.py#L136-L158)

## Architectural Properties and Trade-offs

Several deliberate engineering properties emerge from the code, each with direct operational implications:

| Property | Evidence | Implication |
|---|---|---|
| Single-sequence loop, no batching | `predict.py` iterates `input_datas.items()` one at a time | O(1) peak VRAM per protein; long proteins handled via embedding chunking |
| Inference-only graph | `torch.inference_mode()` in embedder, `no_grad` in `predict_from_x`, `model.eval()` | Minimal activation memory; dropout inert at dropout_rate=0 |
| Explicit VRAM hygiene | `del hidden, input_ids, attention_mask, tok` per chunk | Embeddings of very long proteins stay bounded |
| CPU-anchored weight loading | `map_location='cpu'` then `.to(device)` | Checkpoint is device-portable; no GPU required at load time |
| Gradient firewall between stages | `no_grad` around AF extractor, detached re-anchored leaf | Stage B cannot corrupt Stage A; attribution remains possible |
| Threshold as configuration constant | `threshold = 0.26` set once at facade init | Threshold travels with the model object, shared by writer and decision logic |

The overall design philosophy is clear: a **fixed, frozen feature contract** (the 12-channel structural vector) between a language-model front end and a compact convolutional head. This makes the binding head cheap, the system debuggable at the feature boundary, and the entire pipeline reproducible from a single weight file plus the threshold constant.

Sources: [predict.py](/src/daruma_binding/predict.py#L69-L73), [functions.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/functions.py#L69-L114), [models.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L174-L179)

## Where to Go Next

Follow the data flow downstream through the Deep Dive catalog:

- Go deeper into the neural components in pipeline order: [Convolutional Backbone: FEU and PU](6-convolutional-backbone-feu-and-pu) → [Auxiliary Structural Feature Heads](7-auxiliary-structural-feature-heads) → [Multi-Kernel Conv Binding Head](8-multi-kernel-conv-binding-head)
- Understand the memory/accuracy trade-off inside Stage 2: [ProtT5 Embedding Chunking Strategy](9-prott5-embedding-chunking-strategy)
- Examine how the threshold constant was derived and validated: [Inference Orchestration and Decision Threshold](10-inference-orchestration-and-decision-threshold)
- For practical invocation and output interpretation, return to [Quick Start](2-quick-start) and [Output Format Reference](3-output-format-reference)

# Convolutional Backbone: FEU and PU



This page explains the convolutional backbone of DARUMA-binding: a two-stage, fully convolutional stack named `daruma_like` that transforms per-residue ProtT5 embeddings (1024 channels) into per-residue binding logits. The two stages — the **Feature Extraction Unit (FEU)** and the **Prediction Unit (PU)** — are implemented as explicitly named `nn.Sequential` submodules and define the architectural template that the auxiliary structural heads also inherit. We analyze the layer composition, receptive field geometry, the shape contract enforced by zero-padding, and the parameter budget, at the level of detail required to reason about or modify the network.

Sources: [models.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L82-L114), [predict.py](/src/daruma_binding/predict.py#L58-L61)

## Position in the Architecture: The `daruma_like` Template

The backbone lives in the `daruma_like` class, which extends the minimal base class `myModel`. The base class contributes three infrastructure concerns — weight loading (with a CPU-mapped variant for portable inference), an `in_ch`/`out_ch` channel contract, and a static `logit_to_prob` helper that applies `softmax(logits, dim=-1)[..., 1]` to extract the binding-class probability from the two-channel output. Everything below that is the FEU+PU design itself: `daruma_like.__init__` builds the `self.FEU` and `self.PU` submodules, and its `forward` is a three-line composition of pad → FEU → PU.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class myModel {
        +int in_ch
        +int out_ch
        +_load_weights(path)
        +_load_weights_to_cpu(path)
        +logit_to_prob(logits)$
    }
    class daruma_like {
        +Sequential FEU
        +Sequential PU
        +forward(x) (1, L, out_ch)
    }
    class plddt_daruma_like_ProtT5_nr60
    class rsa_daruma_like_ProtT5_nr60
    class ss8_daruma_like8_ProtT5_nr60
    myModel <|-- daruma_like
    daruma_like <|-- plddt_daruma_like_ProtT5_nr60
    daruma_like <|-- rsa_daruma_like_ProtT5_nr60
    daruma_like <|-- ss8_daruma_like8_ProtT5_nr60
```

This inheritance structure matters for the rest of the "Neural Model Design" section: the pLDDT/RSA/SS8 predictors are **the same FEU+PU backbone with only `out_ch` changed**, wrapped by a separate ensemble class, while the final binding head is a different, multi-kernel design that consumes those heads' outputs rather than reusing FEU/PU directly. Those two systems are documented in [Auxiliary Structural Feature Heads](7-auxiliary-structural-feature-heads) and [Multi-Kernel Conv Binding Head](8-multi-kernel-conv-binding-head) respectively; this page stays strictly within the `daruma_like` template.

Sources: [models.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L63-L114), [models.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L117-L133)

## Feature Extraction Unit (FEU): Local Pattern Compression

The FEU is three identical Conv1d blocks: 1024 → 128, then two 128 → 128 layers, each with `kernel_size=9` and `padding=4` followed by `ReLU(inplace=True)`. The `padding=4` is floor-division padding (`k//2`), which makes every layer **length-preserving** — the FEU never changes the sequence dimension, it only reshapes the channel dimension. Its two jobs are therefore (1) to compress the 1024-dimensional ProtT5 embedding into a 128-channel representation, an 8× reduction that contains the vast majority of the network's first-layer parameters, and (2) to build local motif features by stacking local convolutions.

The receptive field grows linearly with depth: each kernel-9 layer adds 8 positions, so after three layers each FEU output position integrates **1 + 3 × (9−1) = 25 residues** of context (±12 around the residue). This is deliberately modest — the FEU detects local patterns, and long-range aggregation is delegated entirely to the PU. The design pattern is the classic "narrow early, aggregate late" motif of sequence convnets: the expensive 1024×128 projection happens once with a small kernel, and all subsequent layers operate on cheap 128-channel tensors.

| FEU Layer | Operation | Channels | Kernel | Padding | Output Shape |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `FEU[0]` | Conv1d + ReLU | 1024 → 128 | 9 | 4 | `(1, 128, L')` |
| `FEU[2]` | Conv1d + ReLU | 128 → 128 | 9 | 4 | `(1, 128, L')` |
| `FEU[4]` | Conv1d + ReLU | 128 → 128 | 9 | 4 | `(1, 128, L')` |

*`L'` is the padded sequence length (see the shape contract below); the FEU preserves it exactly.*

Sources: [models.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L87-L94)

## Prediction Unit (PU): Global Aggregation and Per-Residue Classification

The PU is a hybrid conv + pointwise-MLP head organized in two halves. The first half is a single **wide, valid** convolution: `Conv1d(128 → 128, kernel_size=121, padding=0)` followed by ReLU and `Dropout(0.5)`. This layer is the network's long-range context mechanism — with a 121-residue window it adds 120 to the receptive field, extending the total to **145 residues (±72)**. Because `padding=0`, this convolution *shrinks* the sequence by 120 positions, a property the forward pass deliberately exploits (next section).

The second half is a per-residue classifier operating in `(B, L, C)` layout: a custom `PermuteLayer(0, 2, 1)` swaps to channels-last, then `Linear(128 → 128)` + ReLU + `Dropout(0.5)` + `Linear(128 → out_ch)`. These linear layers act as **1×1 convolutions** — each residue is classified independently from its 128-dim aggregated feature vector, with no further mixing across positions. The final `out_ch=2` logits are two-class (binding / non-binding) scores, later converted to probabilities by `myModel.logit_to_prob` outside the backbone.

| PU Stage | Operation | Layout | Output Shape | Role |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `PU[0]` | Conv1d + ReLU | channels-first | `(1, 128, L'−120)` | 121-residue context aggregation |
| `PU[2]` | Dropout (p=0.5) | channels-first | `(1, 128, L'−120)` | regularization |
| `PU[3]` | `PermuteLayer(0, 2, 1)` | → channels-last | `(1, L'−120, 128)` | layout switch for Linear |
| `PU[4]` | Linear + ReLU | channels-last | `(1, L'−120, 128)` | non-linear feature refinement |
| `PU[6]` | Dropout (p=0.5) | channels-last | `(1, L'−120, 128)` | regularization |
| `PU[7]` | Linear (128 → out_ch) | channels-last | `(1, L'−120, out_ch)` | per-residue logits |

Note the custom `PermuteLayer` (a thin wrapper around `x.permute(*dims)`) — it exists so the entire PU, including the layout switch, can live inside a single `nn.Sequential`, keeping the forward pass a flat composition.

Sources: [models.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L15-L21), [models.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L96-L106), [models.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L77-L79)

## The Shape Contract: Why Forward Pads Exactly (60, 60)

The `forward` method begins with `F.pad(x, (60, 60), mode="constant", value=0)` before touching any layer. This is not an arbitrary context margin — it is the exact algebraic compensation for the PU's valid convolution, and it is the single most important invariant of the backbone:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Input<br/>(1, 1024, L)"] -->|"F.pad constant 0<br/>60 left + 60 right"| B["(1, 1024, L+120)"]
    B --> C["FEU<br/>3 × Conv1d k=9 p=4<br/>length-preserving"]
    C --> D["(1, 128, L+120)"]
    D --> E["PU: Conv1d k=121<br/>padding=0 (valid)"]
    E --> F["(1, 128, L+120−121+1)<br/>= (1, 128, L)"]
    F --> G["PU: Permute + MLP<br/>per-residue"]
    G --> H["Output<br/>(1, L, out_ch)"]
```

The arithmetic: the input grows by 120 positions; the PU's kernel-121 valid convolution removes exactly 121 − 1 = 120 positions; the FEU layers in between are length-preserving. The result is that **the output length always equals the input length**, residue-for-residue, so binding probabilities from the backbone can be aligned directly with the input sequence without any trimming or bookkeeping. The zeros also serve as a neutral "blank embedding" at sequence termini, letting boundary residues receive a full 145-residue receptive field instead of being truncated.

> [!TIP]
> If you modify the PU's kernel size `K`, you must change the forward padding to `((K−1)//2, (K−1)//2)` — with the current odd `K=121` this is `(60, 60)`. Breaking this pairing silently misaligns the output against the input sequence, which would corrupt every downstream residue-level output written by the predictor.
