Sources: [models.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L108-L114), [models.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L35-L59)

## Input Contract and Parameter Budget

The backbone's input contract is fixed by its instantiators: every `*_daruma_like_ProtT5_nr60` subclass raises `ValueError` unless `in_ch == 1024`, matching the ProtT5 embedding dimension. In the deployed pipeline, `predict.py` constructs a `SequenceFeaturizer(feature_type="ProtT5")` and the wrapper's `predict_from_seq` transposes the featurized sequence into the channels-first `(1, 1024, L)` tensor the backbone expects; the full embedding-to-tensor path is detailed in [ProtT5 Embedding Chunking Strategy](9-prott5-embedding-chunking-strategy) and the surrounding orchestration in [Inference Orchestration and Decision Threshold](10-inference-orchestration-and-decision-threshold).

Despite the wide PU kernel, the total budget is modest at **3,474,306 parameters**, with an interesting distribution: the PU's kernel-121 convolution alone is the single largest layer (1.98M, ~57%), because kernel size multiplies the per-position weight cost — 121 × 16,384 weights versus 9 × 131,072 for the FEU's projection layer. Channel width, not kernel size, dominates the FEU's cost.

| Layer | Parameters | Share |
|---|---|---|
| `FEU[0]` Conv1d 1024→128, k=9 | 1,179,776 | 34.0% |
| `FEU[2]` Conv1d 128→128, k=9 | 147,584 | 4.2% |
| `FEU[4]` Conv1d 128→128, k=9 | 147,584 | 4.2% |
| `PU[0]` Conv1d 128→128, k=121 | 1,982,592 | 57.1% |
| `PU[4]` Linear 128→128 | 16,512 | 0.5% |
| `PU[7]` Linear 128→out_ch | 258 | <0.1% |
| **Total** | **3,474,306** | 100% |

Sources: [models.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L117-L127), [predict.py](/src/daruma_binding/predict.py#L58-L61), [models.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L245-L251)

## Runtime Behavior: Dropout and the Backbone as a Frozen Feature Extractor

Although `daruma_like` defaults to `dropout_rate=0.5`, dropout is **inactive in the deployed system** through two independent mechanisms. First, the top-level wrapper instantiates the whole model with `dropout_rate=0`, and the auxiliary `daruma_like` heads inside it are likewise built with `dropout_rate=0`; second, inference always runs under `torch.no_grad()` with the module in `eval()` mode, which disables dropout regardless. For the binding head, the backbone-derived structural heads are additionally wrapped in `torch.no_grad()` inside `forward` and detached — they act as a **frozen feature extractor**, meaning gradients never flow back through the FEU/PU weights of the auxiliary heads during binding-head inference. The OCCLUSION analysis tooling exploits exactly this: it re-enters the graph at the exposed `af_features` tensor rather than at the raw embeddings.

This page's scope ends at the backbone. How these `daruma_like` instances are composed into the pLDDT/RSA/SS8 ensemble, and how the 12-channel structural feature tensor feeds the multi-kernel binding head, are covered in [Auxiliary Structural Feature Heads](7-auxiliary-structural-feature-heads) and [Multi-Kernel Conv Binding Head](8-multi-kernel-conv-binding-head). For the identical FEU/PU code shipped as the CAID 4 submission snapshot, see [Docker and CAID Usage](4-docker-and-caid-usage).

> [!TIP]
> The CAID directory (`caid/DARUMA-binding/daruma_binding/backend/models.py`) contains a byte-for-byte equivalent FEU/PU implementation — the architecture is intentionally frozen across both entry points. If you ever patch the backbone, both copies must change, or the CAID benchmark results will silently diverge from the `src/` pipeline.


# Auxiliary Structural Feature Heads



Beneath DARUMA-binding's binding head lies a layered feature substrate: three independently trained per-residue predictors that convert ProtT5 embeddings into interpretable structural signals — predicted **pLDDT**, **RSA**, and **eight-state secondary structure (SS8)**. This page dissects how these auxiliary heads are constructed, how their outputs are fused into a 12-channel feature vector, and how that vector is consumed downstream. It sits between the shared convolutional backbone ([Convolutional Backbone: FEU and PU](6-convolutional-backbone-feu-and-pu)) and the specialized binding head ([Multi-Kernel Conv Binding Head](8-multi-kernel-conv-binding-head)). All definitions live in a single file: `src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py`.

## Three Heads, One Backbone: The DAF Predictor Family

The auxiliary heads are three thin specializations of the same `daruma_like` architecture used for binding prediction itself. Each is a standalone residue-level classifier that consumes the same 1024-dimensional ProtT5 embedding and differs **only in output width**: two heads emit binary logits (2 channels), one emits 8-class logits. The repository's data documentation refers to this family as the **DAF models** — DAF-pLDDT, DAF-RSA, and DAF-SS — each with its own training and validation splits archived separately from the binding data. The `nr60` suffix in every class name encodes the training protocol: ProtT5 inputs at 60% sequence-identity redundancy reduction, whose construction details the data documentation defers to the manuscript.

| Class | Task | `out_ch` | Output classes | Dedicated training/validation data |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `plddt_daruma_like_ProtT5_nr60` | pLDDT (high/low confidence) | 2 | 2 | `train/val_plddt.txt` (DAF-pLDDT) |
| `rsa_daruma_like_ProtT5_nr60` | Relative solvent accessibility | 2 | 2 | `train/val_rsa.txt` (DAF-RSA) |
| `ss8_daruma_like8_ProtT5_nr60` | Q8 secondary structure | 8 | 8 | `train/val_ss.txt` (DAF-SS) |

Sources: [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L117-L133), [data/README.md](data/README.md#L11-L27)

The specialization classes are deliberately minimal — each is a constructor that pins `out_ch` (2, 2, 8) and hard-fails if `in_ch` deviates from 1024, protecting the ProtT5 dimensionality contract. Note that the class names carry semantic weight beyond typing: `daruma_like8` for the SS8 head signals its widened output, while every name ending in `ProtT5_nr60` documents the embedding source and redundancy protocol at a glance.

## Class Hierarchy: Specialization by Output Width

The inheritance structure is a textbook example of **template specialization through width**: a fully parameterized base (`daruma_like`, itself extending the weight-loading `myModel`), three zero-logic subclasses that vary only `out_ch`, and two composition classes that aggregate heads or stack them behind the binding head. No auxiliary head redefines `forward` — they inherit the padding → FEU → PU pipeline verbatim from `daruma_like`.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    myModel <|-- daruma_like : base with FEU + PU
    daruma_like <|-- plddt_daruma_like_ProtT5_nr60 : out_ch=2
    daruma_like <|-- rsa_daruma_like_ProtT5_nr60 : out_ch=2
    daruma_like <|-- ss8_daruma_like8_ProtT5_nr60 : out_ch=8
    myModel <|-- af_daruma_like_ProtT5_features : head aggregator
    myModel <|-- af_daruma_like_ProtT5_features_mk1dconv_relu : full binding model
    af_daruma_like_ProtT5_features o-- plddt_daruma_like_ProtT5_nr60
    af_daruma_like_ProtT5_features o-- rsa_daruma_like_ProtT5_nr60
    af_daruma_like_ProtT5_features o-- ss8_daruma_like8_ProtT5_nr60
    af_daruma_like_ProtT5_features_mk1dconv_relu o-- af_daruma_like_ProtT5_features
    af_daruma_like_ProtT5_features_mk1dconv_relu o-- MultiKernelConv1d_withDropout
```

Sources: [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L82-L133), [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L136-L187)

Each head instance is **weight-independent** — the aggregator instantiates three separate `daruma_like` objects, so a pLDDT specialist shares nothing with the RSA specialist despite identical topology. This is parallel ensemble architecture, not shared-trunk multi-task learning: the three tasks were decoupled at training time (each with its own dataset), then coupled at inference time by concatenation.

## The 12-Channel AF Feature Vector

The aggregator `af_daruma_like_ProtT5_features` runs all three heads on the same input, applies `softmax` along the class dimension of each, and concatenates along the feature dimension: 2 (pLDDT) + 2 (RSA) + 8 (SS8) = **12 channels per residue**, shaped `(1, L, 12)`. The channel semantics are codified in the composite model's `af_list` attribute — a self-documenting contract that downstream code indexes against:

| Channels | Labels (`af_list`) | Producer | Consumer |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0–1 | `plddt`, `1-plddt` | pLDDT head softmax | `plddt = ch[0] × 100` |
| 2–3 | `1-rsa`, `rsa` | RSA head softmax | `rsa = ch[3]` |
| 4–11 | `ss0(Alphahelix)` … `ss7(other)` | SS8 head softmax | SS8 output line; Q8→Q3 reduction |

Sources: [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L136-L152), [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L170-L171)

Because each binary head's two softmax channels are complementary, the labels literally read as *p* and *1−p* — but observe the **ordering asymmetry**: for pLDDT the positive class is channel 0, while for RSA it is channel 3. This asymmetry is not a defect; it is the exact indexing convention that `predict_from_x` honours, and misreading it would invert an exported signal.

> [!TIP]
> The channel layout is a positional contract, not a named mapping. `af_list` exists for documentation and future attribution analysis; every consumer in production code uses raw integer indices (`[..., 0]` for pLDDT, `[..., 3]` for RSA, `[..., 4:12]` for SS8). When extending the feature set, insert new channels at the end — reordering would silently corrupt every downstream slice.

## From Standalone Predictors to Frozen Feature Extractor

Inside the production model `af_daruma_like_ProtT5_features_mk1dconv_relu`, the head aggregator runs under `torch.no_grad()`: at inference the heads are a **frozen feature extractor**, not a trainable pathway. Their 12-channel output is then transposed to channels-first `(1, 12, L)` and handed to the multi-kernel convolution stage, which is documented on the next page ([Multi-Kernel Conv Binding Head](8-multi-kernel-conv-binding-head)). The full inference flow, with verified tensor shapes:

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    X["ProtT5 embedding x — (1, 1024, L)"]
    subgraph AGG["af_daruma_like_ProtT5_features — frozen (no_grad)"]
        direction TB
        HP["pLDDT head — (1, L, 2)"] --> SP["softmax"]
        HR["RSA head — (1, L, 2)"] --> SR["softmax"]
        HS["SS8 head — (1, L, 8)"] --> SS["softmax"]
        SP & SR & SS --> CAT["concat dim=2 — (1, L, 12)"]
    end
    X --> HP & HR & HS
    CAT --> D["detach() → requires_grad_(True)"]
    D --> ST["stored as self.af_features"]
    D --> T["transpose — (1, 12, L)"]
    T --> MK["MultiKernelConv1d k∈{3,7,15,31,63,127} — (1, 48, L)"]
    MK --> OUT["1×1 Conv1d — (1, 2, L)"]
```

Sources: [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L156-L187)

The most architecturally significant line in the file is `features.detach().requires_grad_(True)` — executed only when `return_af_features=True`, which the deployed `daruma_binding` wrapper always enables. Detaching makes the feature tensor a **leaf tensor** that gradients can flow *into* (but not through to the frozen heads), and storing it on `self.af_features` preserves it after the forward pass. This is precisely the mechanism that later lets occlusion-based attribution ask: *how much does each of the 12 structural channels contribute to the binding score at this residue?* — the subject of [Occlusion-Based Feature Attribution](15-occlusion-based-feature-attribution).

> [!TIP]
> The `no_grad` → `detach` → `requires_grad_(True)` sequence is not redundant. `no_grad` blocks graph construction inside the heads (memory + speed); `detach` severs the returned tensor from any remaining history; the final `requires_grad_(True)` re-arms it as an autograd leaf so `backward()` on the binding output can compute gradients *with respect to the features themselves*. Delete any one of the three and the attribution workflow breaks.

## Post-Processing: Channel Indexing, Q8→Q3 Reduction, and the Output Surface

The `daruma_binding` wrapper's `predict_from_x` converts raw AF probabilities into the human-facing structural outputs. Three transformations occur: pLDDT channel 0 is **scaled by 100** to recover the conventional 0–100 AlphaFold confidence scale; RSA is read directly from channel 3; and the 8 SS8 probability channels undergo a **Q8→Q3 reduction** by grouped summation — helix = sum of channels 4:7 (H, G, I), sheet = sum of 7:9 (E, B), coil = sum of 9:12 (T, S, coil). The mappings between Q8 indices and one-letter codes are held in `q8_to_char`/`q3_to_char` dictionaries, and `predict_from_seq` renders argmaxed probabilities into `ss8_str`/`ss3_str` strings.

| AF channel | `q8_to_char` | State |
|---|---|---|
| 4 | `H` | Alpha helix |
| 5 | `G` | 3-10 helix |
| 6 | `I` | pi helix |
| 7 | `E` | Extended strand |
| 8 | `B` | Isolated beta bridge |
| 9 | `T` | Turn |
| 10 | `S` | Bend |
| 11 | `-` | Other (coil) |

Sources: [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L222-L240), [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L205-L220)

These derived signals are not internal only — they are a first-class part of the output contract. `ResultWriter` writes them as lines 5–8 of every result file: per-residue pLDDT floats, per-residue RSA floats, an SS3 character string, and an SS8 character string. In other words, users receive the auxiliary heads' predictions as *explainable structural context* alongside the binding probabilities, at no extra inference cost since the heads run anyway to produce the binding model's input features. The full file format is specified in [Output Format Reference](3-output-format-reference).

Sources: [functions.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/functions.py#L133-L160)

## Training Provenance and Naming Conventions

Three facts about how these heads came to be are verifiable in the repository. **First**, each head has dedicated supervision: `data/README.md` lists separate training and validation files for the DAF-pLDDT, DAF-RSA, and DAF-SS models, distinct from the binding data. **Second**, the large training corpora (including `train_plddt.txt`, `train_rsa.txt`, `train_ss.txt`) are archived on Zenodo rather than in-repo, so reproduction requires that download — detailed in [Training Data and Zenodo Archive](12-training-data-and-zenodo-archive). **Third**, dataset construction, redundancy reduction, and splitting are documented in the manuscript, with the `nr60` class-name suffix matching the redundancy-reduction theme. At deployment, inference-time dropout is disabled everywhere (`dropout_rate=0` in both the aggregator's heads and the composite model), consistent with a deterministic `eval()`-mode pipeline assembled by the `daruma_binding` wrapper.

Sources: [data/README.md](data/README.md#L11-L37), [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L136-L142), [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L191-L198)

## Where This Fits in the Pipeline

The auxiliary heads are the **information bottleneck** of DARUMA-binding: 1024 generic embedding dimensions are compressed into 12 interpretable structural channels, and only those channels reach the binding head. Reading onward in catalog order: [Convolutional Backbone: FEU and PU](6-convolutional-backbone-feu-and-pu) details the FEU/PU blocks each head inherits; [Multi-Kernel Conv Binding Head](8-multi-kernel-conv-binding-head) covers the multi-scale convolutions that consume the 12-channel vector; and [Occlusion-Based Feature Attribution](15-occlusion-based-feature-attribution) exploits the stored `af_features` leaf tensor to quantify which structural channel drives each binding prediction.


# Multi-Kernel Conv Binding Head



The multi-kernel conv binding head is the final classification stage of DARUMA-binding: it converts a 12-channel per-residue structural feature vector into 2-way binding logits by fusing evidence from six parallel 1D convolutions with kernel sizes spanning 3 to 127. This page dissects the head's module anatomy, its branch topology and receptive-field design, the frozen-feature contract it enforces on its input, and the integration hooks it exposes to the inference wrapper and the occlusion-attribution pipeline.

## Architectural Position: Where the Head Sits

DARUMA-binding is organized as a two-stage cascade. Stage one — documented in [Convolutional Backbone: FEU and PU](6-convolutional-backbone-feu-and-pu) and [Auxiliary Structural Feature Heads](7-auxiliary-structural-feature-heads) — trains three `daruma_like` networks (pLDDT, RSA, SS8) that map a ProtT5 embedding to per-residue structural probabilities. Stage two is the binding head: the class `af_daruma_like_ProtT5_features_mk1dconv_relu` consumes the concatenated 12-channel output of those three heads (`plddt` + `1-plddt` + `1-rsa` + `rsa` + 8 SS8 states) and produces the final binding/non-binding logits. The stage-one extractor runs entirely under `torch.no_grad()` inside the head's forward pass, so it behaves as a fixed, deterministic feature front-end rather than a trainable component of the binding decision.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph FE["Stage 1: frozen feature extractor"]
        P["pLDDT head"] --> SM1["softmax"]
        R["RSA head"] --> SM2["softmax"]
        S["SS8 head"] --> SM3["softmax"]
        SM1 --> CAT["concat dim=2<br/>12 features / residue"]
        SM2 --> CAT
        SM3 --> CAT
    end
    subgraph HEAD["Stage 2: binding head (this page)"]
        MK["MultiKernelConv1d_withDropout<br/>6 branches, k = 3,7,15,31,63,127"]
        OL["output_layer<br/>Conv1d 48 to 2, k=1"]
    end
    subgraph CONS["Downstream consumers"]
        WRAP["daruma_binding wrapper<br/>softmax + threshold"]
        OCC["Occlusion analysis"]
    end
    CAT -->|"features (1, L, 12)"| MK
    MK -->|"(1, 48, L)"| OL
    OL -->|"logits (1, L, 2)"| WRAP
    MK -.->|"af_features hook"| OCC
```

The head's composition is declared in its constructor: `mk1` (the multi-kernel block), `output_layer` (a single pointwise convolution), and `af_feature_extractor` (the frozen stage-one ensemble), plus the `return_af_features` flag that controls the gradient hook. The 12-channel input ordering is pinned by `af_list`, which documents channel 0 as pLDDT, channel 3 as RSA, and channels 4–11 as the eight Q8 secondary-structure states — an ordering the inference wrapper later relies on when unpacking outputs.

Sources: [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L156-L171), [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L135-L152)

## The Core Module: MultiKernelConv1d_withDropout

`MultiKernelConv1d_withDropout` is a compact fan-out/fan-in primitive: it builds an `nn.ModuleList` of parallel branches, one per requested kernel size, where each branch is `nn.Sequential(Conv1d(in_channels, out_channels, kernel_size=k, padding=k//2), ReLU, Dropout1d)`. Its forward pass runs every branch on the same input tensor and concatenates the results along the channel dimension, producing the shape contract documented in its docstring: input `(B, C_in, L)` maps to output `(B, C_out * len(kernel_sizes), L)`. The constructor enforces that `kernel_sizes` and `dropout_rates` have equal length, making per-branch regularization an explicit, paired configuration rather than a global scalar.

Note that `Dropout1d` is resolved defensively at module import time — `getattr(nn, "Dropout1d", None) or nn.Dropout` — because `nn.Dropout1d` only exists from PyTorch 1.12 onward, while the project's tested environment is PyTorch 1.12.1+cu102. Semantically this matters: `Dropout1d` zeroes entire channels of a `(B, C, L)` tensor, so on these branches it would ablate whole learned feature maps across all residues simultaneously — a channel-wise regularization suited to multi-branch designs where a branch's maps are semantically coherent units.

> [!TIP]
> The concat-along-channels design means the six branches never interact until the output layer — each branch is an independent scale-specific detector, and cross-scale integration happens exactly once, inside the 1×1 output convolution. This is the defining property of the head's inception-style topology.

Sources: [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L13-L59)

## Branch Topology: Receptive Fields as a Design Choice

The deployed configuration instantiates six branches with kernel sizes `[3, 7, 15, 31, 63, 127]`, each mapping the 12 input channels to 8 output channels, each with dropout rate `0.0`, and ReLU enabled. The kernel sizes follow the pattern `2^n − 1`, which is not cosmetic: for odd kernels, symmetric zero padding of `k//2` exactly preserves sequence length, so all six branches produce length-aligned outputs that remain residue-indexed — a precondition for the channel-wise concatenation to be meaningful. Receptive fields therefore range from ±1 residue (short local motifs) to ±63 residues (extended IDR segments), giving the head six distinct context scales without stacking convolutional depth.

| Branch | Kernel size | Padding | Per-side context | Branch output |
|--------|-------------|---------|------------------|---------------|
| 1 | 3 | 1 | ±1 residue | 8 channels |
| 2 | 7 | 3 | ±3 residues | 8 channels |
| 3 | 15 | 7 | ±7 residues | 8 channels |
| 4 | 31 | 15 | ±15 residues | 8 channels |
| 5 | 63 | 31 | ±31 residues | 8 channels |
| 6 | 127 | 63 | ±63 residues | 8 channels |

Six branches × 8 channels = 48 concatenated channels, which is exactly the input width expected by `output_layer = nn.Sequential(Conv1d(48, 2, kernel_size=1))`. This pointwise convolution is the sole point of cross-channel mixing: it learns, per residue, how to weight the 48 scale-specific evidence channels into two logits. Branches use `Conv1d`'s default zero padding, meaning edge residues see zero-padded context rather than replicated boundary values — worth remembering when interpreting predictions near sequence termini.

Sources: [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L160-L164), [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L35-L59)

## Inside the Head: The Forward Pass and the Gradient Hook

The forward pass sequences four operations. First, the frozen extractor computes the 12-channel feature tensor under `torch.no_grad()`, severing the computation graph from stage one. Second — when `return_af_features=True`, as it is in deployment — the features are detached and re-attached to the graph as a fresh leaf via `features.detach().requires_grad_(True)`, then cached on the model as `self.af_features`. Third, the features are transposed to channel-first `(1, 12, L)` and pushed through the six-branch multi-kernel block. Fourth, the 48-channel result passes through the 1×1 output convolution and is transposed back to `(1, L, 2)`.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["x: ProtT5 embedding (1, 1024, L)"] --> B["af_feature_extractor<br/>torch.no_grad"]
    B --> C["features (1, L, 12)"]
    C --> D["detach().requires_grad_(True)<br/>cached as self.af_features"]
    D --> E["transpose (1, 12, L)"]
    E --> F["mk1: 6 parallel branches<br/>k = 3, 7, 15, 31, 63, 127<br/>each: Conv1d 12 to 8 + ReLU + Dropout1d"]
    F --> G["concat dim=1 (1, 48, L)"]
    G --> H["output_layer Conv1d 48 to 2, k=1"]
    H --> I["transpose logits (1, L, 2)"]
```

The `detach().requires_grad_()` pattern is architecturally deliberate. Because stage one is frozen, the binding head is the only differentiable consumer of the features; re-rooting the graph at the feature tensor makes `af_features` a legitimate gradient input. The occlusion-based attribution workflow — detailed in [Occlusion-Based Feature Attribution](15-occlusion-based-feature-attribution) — exploits exactly this: it can perturb the cached feature tensor and backpropagate into it to measure per-channel sensitivity, without ever touching stage-one weights. The wrapper exposes the same tensor read-only via `get_af_features()`.

> [!TIP]
> Observe that the head's `dropout_rate` constructor parameter is effectively vestigial: it is accepted and forwarded to the base class, but the branch dropout rates passed to `mk1` are a hardcoded list of six `0.0` values. In the shipped model, regularization is fully determined by that literal list, not by the parameter — a detail that matters when re-instantiating the architecture for retraining.

Sources: [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L174-L187), [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L192-L193), [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L242-L243)

## Tensor Shape Contract

The head's data flow is length-invariant end to end — every operation either preserves or explicitly restores the residue axis. This is what allows logits to be index-aligned with the original sequence, and what allows the wrapper to unpack `af_features` by absolute channel position.

| Stage | Operation | Tensor shape |
|-------|-----------|--------------|
| Input | ProtT5 embedding | `(1, 1024, L)` |
| Feature extraction | Frozen heads + softmax + concat | `(1, L, 12)` |
| Gradient hook | `detach().requires_grad_()` | `(1, L, 12)` (new graph leaf) |
| Transpose | channel-first | `(1, 12, L)` |
| Multi-kernel block | 6 branches, concat | `(1, 48, L)` |
| Output layer | pointwise Conv1d | `(1, 2, L)` |
| Output | transpose, residue-first logits | `(1, L, 2)` |

Two length-restoration facts underwrite this contract. Upstream, the stage-one `daruma_like` models zero-pad the embedding by 60 on each side and consume it with kernels totaling exactly 120 positions of reduction (three k=9 FEU convolutions plus one k=121 PU convolution), returning the sequence to length L. Downstream, each head branch pads `k//2` on both sides for odd `k`, again preserving L. The head therefore never distorts the residue axis at any scale it inspects.

Sources: [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L174-L187), [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L108-L114)

## Deployment Configuration and Repository Variants

The shipping wrapper `daruma_binding` instantiates the head with `dropout_rate=0, in_ch=1024, return_af_features=True`, loads `model_weights/daruma_binding_weight.pth` onto CPU, calls `.eval()`, and stores the decision threshold of `0.26` — chosen to maximize F1 on validation data (thresholding itself is covered in [Inference Orchestration and Decision Threshold](10-inference-orchestration-and-decision-threshold)). The state dict covers the entire cascade, frozen extractor included; only execution-time `no_grad` enforcement keeps stage one out of any gradient computation.

The repository carries two near-identical copies of the model code, and their divergence is instructive:

| Aspect | `src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py` (canonical) | `caid/.../backend/models.py` (CAID 4 submission) |
|--------|-----------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------|
| Head class | Identical: same kernel sizes, channel counts, hook | Identical |
| Wrapper constructor | Accepts injected `featurizer` | No featurizer parameter |
| Posterior smoothing | `MovingAverageSmoothing(kernel_size=1)` — disabled | `MovingAverageSmoothing(kernel_size=7)` |
| Feature-order metadata | Declares `af_list` channel labels | Absent |

The `caid/` tree is the frozen code submitted to CAID 4 (per the repository README) and retains the k=7 smoothing window that the canonical `src/` version has since disabled. The canonical version additionally formalizes the 12-channel ordering as `af_list` and supports featurizer injection via `predict_from_seq`, which featurizes a raw sequence to a `(1, D, L)` embedding before invoking the head.

Sources: [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L191-L200), [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L245-L257), [models.py](caid/DARUMA-binding/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L186-L194), [README.md](README.md#L84-L86)

## Downstream Integration: What the Head Exposes

The wrapper's `predict_from_x` treats the head's logits as the sole classification signal and the cached `af_features` as an interpretable byproduct: logits pass through `logit_to_prob` (softmax over the last axis, keeping index 1 as binding probability), while the `(1, L, 12)` feature tensor is squeezed and unpacked by absolute channel index — `[..., 0]` as pLDDT (scaled ×100), `[..., 3]` as RSA, `[..., 4:12]` as the eight SS8 probabilities, with channels 4–6, 7–8, and 9–11 summed into helix/sheet/coil for SS3. This unpacking is only safe because `af_list` guarantees the channel ordering established at head construction — the multi-kernel head and the output writer are coupled by that implicit contract.

For attribution workflows, the head offers two access paths to the same tensor: the in-place cache `self.model.af_features` and the accessor `get_af_features()`. Both hand consumers a graph leaf rooted at the head's input, which is the entry point occlusion analysis perturbs when measuring which structural features drive binding predictions — the mechanism explored in [Occlusion-Based Feature Attribution](15-occlusion-based-feature-attribution).

Sources: [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L222-L243), [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L170-L171)

## Key Takeaways and Where to Go Next

Three properties define this head. It is **scale-decomposed**: six parallel kernels from 3 to 127 capture motif-scale through segment-scale context, with cross-scale fusion deferred entirely to a single 1×1 convolution. It is **frozen-input**: stage-one structural predictions enter under `no_grad`, so the head's trainable surface is exactly the multi-kernel branches plus the pointwise output layer. It is **attribution-ready**: the `detach().requires_grad_()` hook turns its input features into a gradient-addressable leaf, making the head not just a classifier but a designed interface for interpretability.

Recommended reading progression from here:

- Revisit the frozen upstream heads consumed by this page: [Auxiliary Structural Feature Heads](7-auxiliary-structural-feature-heads) and their shared backbone [Convolutional Backbone: FEU and PU](6-convolutional-backbone-feu-and-pu)
- Understand how the head's outputs are smoothed, thresholded, and written: [Inference Orchestration and Decision Threshold](10-inference-orchestration-and-decision-threshold)
- See the gradient hook exploited in practice: [Occlusion-Based Feature Attribution](15-occlusion-based-feature-attribution)
- For the embedding side that feeds stage one: [ProtT5 Embedding Chunking Strategy](9-prott5-embedding-chunking-strategy)


# ProtT5 Embedding Chunking Strategy



This page explains how DARUMA-binding converts arbitrarily long amino acid sequences into fixed-width ProtT5 embeddings without exhausting GPU memory or corrupting residue-level alignment. The strategy lives entirely in the `ProtT5Embedder` class of the standalone pipeline: long sequences are encoded as **overlapping 2048-residue windows**, each window's boundary-contaminated vectors are **trimmed**, and the surviving vectors are **concatenated into a single `(L, 1024)` tensor** that is bit-exactly what a full-length encode would need to produce. Chunking is invisible to the binding network itself — it is a pure embedding-stage concern.

Sources: [functions.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/functions.py#L26-L120), [predict.py](/src/daruma_binding/predict.py#L54-L71)

## Why Long Sequences Force a Chunked Encoder

Self-attention cost and activation memory grow with sequence length, so running a T5 XL encoder over a 20,000-residue protein in one shot is impractical on typical hardware. DARUMA-binding resolves this at the featurization layer: `SequenceFeaturizer` instantiates `ProtT5Embedder` with a hardwired window size, and the binding network downstream always receives the complete protein as one tensor of shape `(1, 1024, L)`. The architecture therefore decouples *encoder context* (bounded per window) from *model receptive field* (full sequence, via the convolutional trunk). The full pipeline positions chunking as follows:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["FASTA input"] --> B["read_fasta<br/>UBJOZ → X"]
    B --> C["ProtT5Embedder.embed()"]
    C -->|"windows of 2048 aa<br/>stride 1536"| D["T5 Encoder<br/>prot_t5_xl_half, fp16"]
    D --> E["last_hidden_state<br/>slice off EOS token"]
    E --> F["Trim 256 vectors<br/>at each seam"]
    F --> G["torch.cat → (L, 1024)"]
    G --> H["predict_from_seq<br/>→ (1, 1024, L), fp32"]
    H --> I["Binding network<br/>FEU → PU → heads"]
```

Two structural facts anchor this design. First, the encoder is `Rostlab/prot_t5_xl_half_uniref50-enc`, loaded in half precision and eval mode, with a CPU fallback that upcasts to float32. Second, every residue is tokenized individually (space-joined string), so the token count per window equals the residue count plus tokenizer special tokens — the basis of the exact residue-to-vector alignment described below.

Sources: [functions.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/functions.py#L26-L59), [functions.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/functions.py#L123-L133), [models.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L245-L257)

## Window Geometry: chunk_size, overlap, trim, step

The constructor takes four interlocking parameters and enforces two invariants that make the whole scheme mathematically sound:

| Parameter | Default value | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `chunk_size` | 2048 | Residues per encoder window |
| `overlap` | 512 | Shared context band between adjacent windows |
| `trim` | `overlap // 2` = 256 | Vectors discarded at each seam before concatenation |
| `step` | `chunk_size - overlap` = 1536 | Stride between window starts |

The two assertions are not stylistic — they encode correctness conditions. `overlap < chunk_size` guarantees `step ≥ 1`, so the loop always makes forward progress. `overlap % 2 == 0` guarantees the overlap band can be split symmetrically into `trim` residues on each side, which is precisely what makes adjacent windows' kept regions abut with no gap and no duplication (proven in the stitching section below). `SequenceFeaturizer` fixes `chunk_size=2048, overlap=512` at construction; there is currently no CLI override.

| Constraint | Assertion | Consequence if violated |
|---|---|---|
| Forward progress | `overlap < chunk_size` | `step ≤ 0` → infinite loop |
| Seamless stitching | `overlap % 2 == 0` | Asymmetric trim → off-by-N misalignment between chunks |

Sources: [functions.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/functions.py#L27-L42), [functions.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/functions.py#L66), [functions.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/functions.py#L127)

## The Chunk Embedding Loop

The `embed()` method iterates windows under a single `torch.inference_mode()` context. The loop is short enough to reason about completely:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S["start = 0, idx = 0"] --> W{"start < L ?"}
    W -->|no| CAT["torch.cat → (L, 1024)"]
    W -->|yes| E["end = min(start + 2048, L)"]
    E --> T["tokenize space-joined slice<br/>add_special_tokens=True"]
    T --> H["T5 forward → last_hidden_state"]
    H --> SL["residue = hidden[0, :end−start]"]
    SL --> TR{"idx == 0 ?"}
    TR -->|first chunk| K1["keep [0 : end−start−256]<br/>if also last chunk: keep all"]
    TR -->|later chunks| K2["keep [256 : end−start−256]<br/>if last chunk: keep through end"]
    K1 --> BUF["detach (+cpu if return_cpu)<br/>del hidden, input_ids, mask"]
    K2 --> BUF
    BUF --> C2{"end == L ?"}
    C2 -->|yes| CAT
    C2 -->|no| ADV["start += 1536, idx += 1"] --> W
```

Three details deserve attention. First, sequences are sanitized twice — non-standard residues `[UBJOZ]` are mapped to `X` at FASTA load, and `[UZOB]` are re-mapped to `X` inside `embed()`, making the embedder robust even when called directly on raw strings. Second, `padding=False` and batch size 1 mean every token position in the window is a real residue except the appended EOS. Third, the chunk index `idx` distinguishes the first window only; its trim policy handles both the "first chunk followed by more" case and the degenerate "single chunk covers everything" case (`L ≤ 2048`).

> [!TIP]
> The slice `residue = hidden[0, :(end - start), :]` exists because `add_special_tokens=True` makes the T5 tokenizer append `</s>` after the last residue, producing `end − start + 1` hidden states. Slicing to `end − start` discards that EOS vector and restores 1:1 residue-to-vector alignment. Delete this slice and every chunk after the first shifts by one residue — the concatenation would still "succeed" while silently corrupting the sequence.

Sources: [functions.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/functions.py#L61-L90), [functions.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/functions.py#L92-L114), [functions.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/functions.py#L12-L23)

## Seam Trimming: Keeping Only Context-Deep Vectors

Each window produces a hidden state for every residue it contains, but vectors near a window's edge were computed with truncated flanking context — the encoder never saw what lies beyond the window. The trim policy discards exactly those vectors and keeps only positions whose encoder context is deep on every emitted side:

| Chunk position | Kept window-local slice | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| First chunk (`idx == 0`), not last | `[0, end − 256)` | N-terminus needs no left context; drop 256 seam-side vectors |
| First chunk, also last (`L ≤ 2048`) | `[0, end)` | No seam exists — keep everything |
| Interior chunks | `[256, end − 256)` | Every kept vector has ≥ 256 residues of encoder context on both sides |
| Final chunk (not first) | `[256, end)` | C-terminus needs no right context; drop 256 seam-side vectors |

The consequence is a strong quality invariant: **every emitted vector comes from a window in which the residue has at least 256 flanking residues encoded on any side that actually exists in the protein.** A vector is only discarded when its window truncated real sequence context. The 512-residue overlap is thus not redundant output — it is *context insurance*: each seam region is encoded twice, once as the tail context of window *k* and once as the head context of window *k+1*, and the higher-quality interior copy survives.

Sources: [functions.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/functions.py#L41-L42), [functions.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/functions.py#L92-L99)

## Lossless Stitching: The Abutment Invariant

Trimming only works if the kept regions tile the sequence exactly. They do, and the arithmetic is checkable. For interior chunk *k* starting at `start_k = 1536k`, the kept slice in global coordinates is:

```
kept(k) = [start_k + 256, start_k + 2048 − 256)
        = [1536k + 256,  1536(k+1) + 256)
```

The end of `kept(k)` equals the start of `kept(k+1)` — the kept regions form a perfect partition of `[256, L)` with zero gaps and zero overlaps, capped on the left by chunk 0's kept region `[0, 1792)`. A concrete trace for a protein of `L = 5000` (which yields `n = ⌈5000/1536⌉ = 4`? no — verify: starts are 0, 1536, 3072, and the window at 3072 reaches 5000, so `n = 3`):

| Chunk | Window `[start, end)` | Kept (global) | Emitted positions | Count |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | [0, 2048) | [0, 1792) | 0 – 1791 | 1792 |
| 1 | [1536, 3584) | [1792, 3328) | 1792 – 3327 | 1536 |
| 2 | [3072, 5000) | [3328, 5000) | 3328 – 4999 | 1672 |
| **Total** | 6024 encoded | — | **0 – 4999** | **5000 = L** ✓ |

The cost side of the ledger: 6024 residues were encoded to emit 5000 vectors — the 1024 encoded-twice residues are the two 512-residue overlap bands. In general, roughly `512·(n−1)` extra residues are encoded (less when the final window is shorter than the overlap), a bounded, predictable redundancy that buys context depth at every seam. Note that a chunk shorter than `chunk_size` can only be the final one: `end < start + 2048` implies `end == L`, so the trim policy's "if last chunk, keep through end" branch is the only variable-length case the loop must handle.

> [!TIP]
> The abutment identity `start_k + chunk_size − trim = start_{k+1} + trim` holds *because* `trim = overlap // 2`. This is the concrete reason the constructor asserts `overlap % 2 == 0`: with an odd overlap, the trim budget cannot split evenly, kept regions would overlap or gap by one residue, and `torch.cat` would silently produce an `(L ± 1, 1024)` tensor that breaks the sequence-length check downstream.

Sources: [functions.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/functions.py#L66-L73), [functions.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/functions.py#L92-L116)

## Precision and Memory Discipline

Chunking alone bounds the *sequence* dimension; the implementation also bounds the *per-window* memory footprint so peak VRAM depends on `chunk_size`, not `L`. The measures, all visible in the code:

| Mechanism | Implementation | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| Half-precision weights | `.half().to(device).eval()` | XL encoder resident in half the memory; matches the `*_half` checkpoint |
| CPU fallback | `self.model.float()` when device is CPU | fp16 matmul is unsupported/slow on CPU |
| Whole-loop inference mode | single `with torch.inference_mode()` | No autograd graph across any chunk |
| Per-chunk teardown | `del hidden, input_ids, attention_mask, tok` | Activations freed before the next window is encoded |
| Optional CPU offload | `return_cpu` flag (default `False`) | Kept chunks stay on GPU for a single device-side `torch.cat` |
| Async host-to-device | `non_blocking=True` transfers | Overlaps copy with compute |

One precision transition is deliberate and easy to miss: embeddings are computed in fp16 but the binding model runs in fp32. `predict_from_seq` upcasts with `.to(torch.float32)` immediately after the permute, so the numerical contract of the trained conv weights is preserved even though their inputs were produced by a half-precision encoder.

Sources: [functions.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/functions.py#L49-L59), [functions.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/functions.py#L69-L108), [models.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L249)

## Integration Contract: From `(L, 1024)` to the Binding Network

The chunking strategy is encapsulated behind a one-call interface. `ProtT5Embedder.__call__` delegates to `embed()`, `SequenceFeaturizer` exposes `featurize(seq)`, and the `daruma_binding` wrapper invokes it in `predict_from_seq`:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["ProtT5Embedder<br/>(L, 1024) fp16"] --> B["featurize(seq)<br/>SequenceFeaturizer"]
    B --> C["unsqueeze(0).permute(0,2,1)<br/>.to(float32)"]
    C --> D["(1, 1024, L)"]
    D --> E["daruma binding model<br/>in_ch = 1024"]
```

The width 1024 is not coincidental — it is `d_model` of `prot_t5_xl`, and every binding-head variant in `models.py` validates `in_ch == 1024`, raising `ValueError` otherwise. The downstream network then pads ±60 and runs FEU/PU convolutions over the *entire* sequence at once; per-residue outputs at position 0 and position L−1 are therefore informed by global context via the conv trunk, compensating for the fact that chunking only constrained the *embedding* stage.

A contrasting integration exists in the CAID 4 submission package: `caid/DARUMA-binding/daruma_binding/predict.py` accepts **pre-computed** ProtT5 vectors as a `.npy` file, validates `X.shape[0] == len(seq)`, and contains no embedder at all. Chunking is a feature of the standalone end-to-end pipeline only — a distinction that matters when reproducing benchmarks via the CAID harness.

| Aspect | Standalone pipeline (`src/`) | CAID package (`caid/`) |
|---|---|---|
| Input | Raw FASTA sequences | Pre-computed ProtT5 `.npy` |
| ProtT5 encoding | Internal, chunked (`ProtT5Embedder`) | Not performed; delegated to the caller |
| Chunking parameters | `chunk_size=2048, overlap=512` | Not applicable |
| Length validation | Guaranteed by construction | Explicit `X.shape[0] != len(seq)` check |

Sources: [functions.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/functions.py#L119-L133), [models.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L83-L121), [models.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L245-L257), [predict.py](/caid/DARUMA-binding/daruma_binding/predict.py#L69-L87), [predict.py](/src/daruma_binding/predict.py#L66-L71)

## Tuning Considerations and Trade-offs

Although `SequenceFeaturizer` hardwires the defaults, the `ProtT5Embedder` constructor exposes the knobs, and their trade-space is worth understanding before changing anything:

| Adjustment | Gain | Cost / Risk |
|---|---|---|
| Smaller `chunk_size` | Lower peak VRAM; runs on smaller GPUs | More chunks, more seams; trim regions re-encoded more often |
| Larger `overlap` | Deeper encoder context at seams → more stable boundary vectors | More duplicated compute (≈ `overlap` residues per seam encoded twice) |
| Smaller `overlap` | Less redundant encoding | Vectors near seams computed with thin flanking context |
| Odd `overlap` | — | Blocked by assertion; breaks the abutment invariant |

The default `(2048, 512)` reflects a deliberate middle point: 1536 useful residues of forward progress per encoder pass, 256 residues of retained context beyond every emitted vector's window edge, and total redundancy confined to the seam bands. Note the loop's per-window cost is dominated by the T5 forward pass; the Python-side slicing, trimming, and `torch.cat` are negligible by comparison.

Sources: [functions.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/functions.py#L27-L42), [functions.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/functions.py#L123-L133)

## Where to Go Next

Chunking is the bridge between the protein language model and the neural predictor. To see where the stitched `(L, 1024)` tensor travels next — through the FEU/PU convolutional trunk, the auxiliary structural-feature heads, and the multi-kernel binding head — continue with [Prediction Pipeline Architecture](5-prediction-pipeline-architecture), [Convolutional Backbone: FEU and PU](6-convolutional-backbone-feu-and-pu), and [Multi-Kernel Conv Binding Head](8-multi-kernel-conv-binding-head). For how the resulting per-residue probabilities are thresholded and written out, see [Inference Orchestration and Decision Threshold](10-inference-orchestration-and-decision-threshold). If you intend to reproduce CAID benchmark results with externally generated embeddings, [Docker and CAID Usage](4-docker-and-caid-usage) covers the precomputed-`.npy` workflow described above.


# Inference Orchestration and Decision Threshold



This page explains how DARUMA-binding turns a trained network into a per-residue prediction workflow: how sequences flow through the featurizer and the model controller, how raw logits become binding probabilities, and how those probabilities are binarized at the decision threshold of **0.26**. It covers the orchestration layers shared by the main package (`src/daruma_binding/`) and the CAID 4 submission (`caid/DARUMA-binding/`), including the one deliberate behavioral difference between them. Model internals (FEU/PU blocks, the multi-kernel conv head) are out of scope here — see [Convolutional Backbone: FEU and PU](6-convolutional-backbone-feu-and-pu) and [Multi-Kernel Conv Binding Head](8-multi-kernel-conv-binding-head).

Sources: [predict.py](src/daruma_binding/predict.py#L1-L17), [README.md](README.md#L22-L37)

## Three Orchestration Layers

Inference is organized into three cooperating layers with a clean separation of concerns. The **entry layer** (`predict.py`) resolves the compute device, reads the FASTA file into an accession→sequence dictionary, and iterates over proteins one at a time. The **controller layer** (`daruma_binding` class in `models.py`) owns the decision policy — the threshold and the probability smoother — and exposes two prediction entry points: `predict_from_seq(seq)` for raw sequences and `predict_from_x(x)` for pre-computed embeddings. The **featurization layer** (`SequenceFeaturizer` wrapping `ProtT5Embedder`) converts a sequence string into a `(L, 1024)` ProtT5 embedding using chunked inference with 2048-residue windows and 512-residue overlap.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["FASTA file (-i)"] --> B["read_fasta()<br/>dict {accession: sequence}"]
    B --> C["daruma_binding controller<br/>weights → device → eval()<br/>threshold = 0.26"]
    C --> D["SequenceFeaturizer<br/>ProtT5 chunked embedding<br/>chunk 2048 / overlap 512"]
    D --> E["predict_from_seq<br/>(L, 1024) → (1, 1024, L) float32"]
    E --> F["predict_from_x<br/>torch.no_grad()"]
    F --> G["network forward<br/>logits (1, L, 2)"]
    G --> H["softmax(dim=-1)[..., 1]<br/>binding probability (L,)"]
    H --> I["MovingAverageSmoothing<br/>kernel_size = 1 (identity)"]
    I --> J["cpu().numpy() → (L,)"]
    J --> K{"prob &gt; 0.26 ?"}
    K -- "yes" --> L["binary_binding = 1"]
    K -- "no" --> M["binary_binding = 0"]
    L --> N["ResultWriter.append_write<br/>8-line block per protein"]
    M --> N
```

Note that the featurizer is injected into the controller at construction time (`daruma_binding(device, featurizer=featurizer)`); the entry script never calls it directly. This injection pattern is what allows the CAID submission to reuse the identical controller with externally pre-computed `.npy` embeddings instead of raw sequences.

Sources: [predict.py](src/daruma_binding/predict.py#L44-L71), [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L191-L257), [functions.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/functions.py#L123-L133), [functions.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/functions.py#L27-L42)

## Per-Protein Execution Sequence

The runtime interaction between the four participants follows a strict sequence. Weights are loaded to CPU first (`_load_weights_to_cpu` with `map_location='cpu'`) and then moved to the target device — a portable loading order that works regardless of the machine that trained the checkpoint. The controller sets the network to `eval()` mode, and both gradient-suppression mechanisms are used deliberately: `torch.inference_mode()` inside the ProtT5 embedder's chunk loop and `torch.no_grad()` around the entire `predict_from_x` call.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant O as predict.py (entry layer)
    participant M as daruma_binding (controller)
    participant F as SequenceFeaturizer → ProtT5Embedder
    participant N as Network (eval mode)
    participant W as ResultWriter

    O->>O: read_fasta → {ac: seq}
    O->>M: daruma_binding(device, featurizer)
    Note over M: weights → CPU → to(device) → eval()<br/>threshold = 0.26, smoother(k=1)
    loop for each protein
        O->>M: predict_from_seq(seq)
        M->>F: featurize(seq)
        F-->>M: embedding (L, 1024), inference_mode
        M->>M: unsqueeze(0).permute → (1, 1024, L)
        M->>N: forward under torch.no_grad()
        N-->>M: logits (1, L, 2) + af_features stored
        M->>M: softmax → class-1 → smoother → prob > 0.26
        M-->>O: result dict
        O->>W: append_write(ac, result, threshold)
        W-->>O: 8-line block appended
    end
```

The orchestration contract is a strict **per-residue alignment**: a sequence of L residues produces exactly L probabilities and L binary predictions, because the network's internal padding and kernel geometry preserve sequence length. The controller guarantees the input cast to `float32` (ProtT5 embeddings are produced in half precision on GPU), and `predict_from_seq` additionally guards against a missing featurizer by raising a `ValueError` before any tensor work begins.

Sources: [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L191-L203), [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L245-L257), [functions.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/functions.py#L61-L117), [predict.py](src/daruma_binding/predict.py#L60-L71)

## From Logits to Binding Probability

The network emits two raw scores per residue with shape `(1, L, 2)`. The controller converts these to a probability via the shared `logit_to_prob` static method: `torch.softmax(logits, dim=-1)[..., 1]` — applying softmax across the two classes, then selecting the class-1 column, which corresponds to the *binding* state. The result is a length-L tensor where each element is P(binding | residue).

A subtle but important point for reproducibility: the softmax is applied **inside** `predict_from_x` after the forward pass, so the value written to output files is always a properly normalized probability, not a raw logit. This makes the downstream threshold comparison meaningful in absolute terms and lets downstream consumers compare probabilities against 0.26 without needing access to the model's score calibration.

Sources: [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L77-L79), [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L222-L228)

## Probability Smoothing: Identity by Default, Active in CAID

Both orchestration variants route the probability curve through a `MovingAverageSmoothing` object before thresholding, but with different kernel sizes. The smoother replicate-pads the sequence (preserving boundary values), unfolds it into overlapping windows via `tensor.unfold`, and averages each window. In the main package the smoother is instantiated with `kernel_size=1` — a mathematical identity, effectively disabling smoothing (the code comment reads "No smoothing for now"). The CAID submission ships with `kernel_size=7`, producing a 7-residue moving average that dampens isolated probability spikes before binarization.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Z["logits (1, L, 2)<br/>raw network output"] -->|"softmax(dim=-1)"| P["prob = class-1 column<br/>P(binding | residue)"]
    P -->|"replicate-pad → unfold → mean"| S["smoothed prob<br/>k=1: unchanged (main)<br/>k=7: 7-residue MA (CAID)"]
    S -->|"int(prob &gt; 0.26)"| T["binary_binding (L,)<br/>1 = binding, 0 = non-binding"]
    P -.->|"exported as-is"| O["output file: binding probability line"]
    T -.->|"exported as-is"| O
```

This is the only behavioral divergence between the two shipped orchestration paths: probabilities published by the standalone package are raw network outputs, while CAID benchmark outputs are smoothed. Note that the raw (unsmoothed) probabilities are exported either way — smoothing affects only the binary line of the output, not the float probability line.

Sources: [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L24-L32), [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L198-L200), [models.py](caid/DARUMA-binding/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L23-L32), [models.py](caid/DARUMA-binding/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L193-L194)

## The Decision Threshold: 0.26

The decision threshold is the constant `self.threshold = 0.26`, annotated in the source with its provenance: *"The threshold of 0.26 is used, which maximizes the F1 score on the validation data."* It was therefore not chosen arbitrarily but tuned on the validation split (see [Training Data and Zenodo Archive](12-training-data-and-zenodo-archive) and [Evaluation Metrics: AUC, APS, Fmax](14-evaluation-metrics-auc-aps-fmax) for how F1-based selection interacts with the other reported metrics). The README confirms this value as the user-facing contract for the binary output line.

Binarization is applied at the **probability level, after smoothing**, using a **strict greater-than** comparison: `(prob > self.threshold).astype(int)`. A residue with probability exactly 0.260000 is classified as non-binding. The threshold is hard-coded in the controller class — neither entry point exposes it as a CLI argument — so tuning it requires editing `models.py` directly. For traceability, the threshold value is not silent: `ResultWriter` embeds it into the output file's comment header (`# Line4. ... threshold=0.26`), so every prediction file documents the exact rule used to derive its binary line.

| Call site | Expression | Binary dtype |
|---|---|---|
| Main package, `predict_from_x` | `(prob > self.threshold).astype(int)` | `int` |
| CAID controller, `predict_from_x` | `(prob > self.threshold).float()` | `float` |
| CAID entry script, output loop | `1 if p > model.threshold else 0` | `int` |

All three sites use the same strict `>` semantics, so a probability of exactly 0.26 is non-binding everywhere. The CAID entry script re-applies the threshold per residue when writing output (its `predict_from_x` returns a `(prob, pred)` tuple, and the writer recomputes the flag from `model.threshold`), keeping the controller and the file format in lockstep even if one is modified.

> [!TIP]
> The threshold lives in exactly one place per package — `models.py` (line 198 in `src/`, line 193 in `caid/`) — and is intentionally not CLI-configurable. If you adjust it, regenerate output files: the `ResultWriter` header stamps the threshold it was constructed with, so stale files expose stale thresholds, which is precisely what makes the header a useful audit trail.

Sources: [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L198), [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L229), [models.py](caid/DARUMA-binding/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L196-L204), [predict.py](caid/DARUMA-binding/daruma_binding/predict.py#L96-L103), [functions.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/functions.py#L136-L147), [README.md](README.md#L52)

## Side-Channel Feature Extraction

Because the binding head consumes predicted structural features internally (see [Auxiliary Structural Feature Heads](7-auxiliary-structural-feature-heads)), the same forward pass that produces binding logits also produces the 12-channel feature tensor. When the network is constructed with `return_af_features=True`, its `forward()` stores the detached features on `self.af_features` — requiring gradients so that occlusion-based attribution can flow through them later. The controller then *reads back* this attribute after the forward call, slicing channels into interpretable outputs and scaling them into human-usable units.

| Feature | Channel slice | Post-processing |
|---|---|---|
| pLDDT | channel 0 (`plddt`) | × 100 to map to the 0–100 scale |
| RSA | channel 3 (`rsa`) | exported as-is |
| SS8 | channels 4–11 | argmax → one of 8 letters via `q8_to_char` |
| SS3 | helix = Σ channels 4–6, sheet = Σ channels 7–8, coil = Σ channels 9–12 | argmax → `H`/`S`/`C` via `q3_to_char` |

The channel ordering matches the documented `af_list` in the network (`plddt, 1-plddt, 1-rsa, rsa, ss0…ss7`), and the SS3 aggregation follows the standard collapse of eight DSSP states into three (the three helix states fold into `H`, `E`+`B` into `S`, the rest into `C`). The full result dictionary — `binding`, `binary_binding`, `plddt`, `rsa`, `ss8`, `ss3`, plus `seq` and the decoded `ss3_str`/`ss8_str` strings added by `predict_from_seq` — is what `ResultWriter` serializes into the eight-line-per-protein output block described in [Output Format Reference](3-output-format-reference).

> [!TIP]
> `predict_from_x` is stateful with respect to the last forward pass: it reads `self.model.af_features` populated during `forward()`, never as a return value. If you batch multiple sequences or reuse the controller, always consume the result dict immediately after each `predict_from_x` call — the side channel is overwritten on the next forward and `get_af_features()` will silently return features from the previous protein.

Sources: [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L156-L181), [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L170-L171), [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L222-L257), [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L205-L220)

## Main Package vs. CAID Submission: Orchestration Variants

The two shipped orchestration paths wrap the same controller logic but diverge in input mode, output contract, and smoothing policy. Understanding this table clarifies which artifacts in `reproduction/` were generated under which smoothing regime (see [Reproducing Paper Figures and Tables](13-reproducing-paper-figures-and-tables)).

| Property | Main package (`src/`) | CAID 4 submission (`caid/`) |
|---|---|---|
| Input mode | FASTA + built-in ProtT5 featurizer | Pre-computed `.npy` ProtT5 vectors |
| Featurizer | Injected, required | Absent (embeddings loaded directly) |
| Threshold | 0.26 | 0.26 |
| Smoother kernel | 1 (identity — disabled) | 7 (active moving average) |
| `predict_from_x` return | Result dict (6 keys) | Tuple `(prob, pred)` |
| Binary dtype | `int` | `float` |
| Batch handling | Loop over FASTA dict, per-protein | Single protein per invocation |
| Device default | GPU `0`, CPU fallback | `cpu`, CUDA opt-in |
| Threading | Library defaults | OMP/MKL pinned to 8, interop = 1 |
| Length validation | Implicit | Explicit `ValueError` (FASTA vs. `.npy` mismatch) |
| Output format | 8-line block per protein | 4 columns per residue (CAID style) |

The CAID variant's design constraints are visible in its entry script: thread counts are pinned before `torch` is imported for deterministic resource usage in the benchmark harness, the embedding tensor is validated against the optional FASTA sequence length, and a dash placeholder sequence is synthesized if no FASTA is supplied (so the residue column can still be written). These are benchmark-environment concerns rather than changes to the decision policy — the softmax → smooth → threshold sequence is identical in both variants.

Sources: [models.py](caid/DARUMA-binding/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L186-L204), [predict.py](caid/DARUMA-binding/daruma_binding/predict.py#L26-L37), [predict.py](caid/DARUMA-binding/daruma_binding/predict.py#L70-L103), [predict.py](src/daruma_binding/predict.py#L31-L71)

## Where to Go Next

To understand how the ProtT5 embeddings feeding this pipeline are produced under GPU memory constraints, continue with [ProtT5 Embedding Chunking Strategy](9-prott5-embedding-chunking-strategy). For the exact serialization of the result dictionary into files, see [Output Format Reference](3-output-format-reference). To understand why 0.26 optimizes F1 and how that trade-off appears against AUC and APS, read [Evaluation Metrics: AUC, APS, Fmax](14-evaluation-metrics-auc-aps-fmax). Finally, the gradient-enabled `af_features` side channel described above is the foundation for [Occlusion-Based Feature Attribution](15-occlusion-based-feature-attribution).

# CAID Benchmark Datasets



This page explains the three community-benchmark test sets under `data/test/` — their file format, the semantic difference between the Binding and Binding-IDR challenges, and how they flow into the evaluation scripts that reproduce the manuscript's headline numbers. These files are the *scoring instruments* of the repository: everything the model claims about binding-region prediction is measured against them. They are deliberately kept separate from training and validation data, whose provenance is covered in [Training Data and Zenodo Archive](12-training-data-and-zenodo-archive).

## The Three Benchmark Sets at a Glance

CAID (Critical Assessment of protein Intrinsic Disorder prediction) is a community-run evaluation in which predictors submit outputs for a fixed target set via the CAID Web Portal; the repository's README confirms all three test files were obtained from that portal. The repo ships one file per challenge edition: CAID 2's Binding challenge, CAID 3's Binding challenge, and CAID 3's Binding-IDR challenge. Each file follows the same underlying record format, which makes them directly interchangeable as scoring targets.

| File | Challenge | Targets | Record format | Role in repo |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `caid2_binding.fasta` | CAID 2 Binding | 78 proteins (accessions `DP02342`–`DP03739`) | 3-line record | Ground-truth labels for CAID 2 evaluation |
| `caid3_binding.fasta` | CAID 3 Binding | 52 proteins (accessions `DP03818`–`DP04391`) | 3-line record | Ground-truth labels for CAID 3 evaluation |
| `caid3_binding_idr.fasta` | CAID 3 Binding-IDR | Same 52 proteins as above | 3-line record with `-` mask | Same labels, but evaluation restricted to annotated disordered regions |

The target counts are verifiable from file structure: `caid2_binding.fasta` spans 235 lines = 78 records × 3 lines + 1 trailing blank, and `caid3_binding.fasta` spans 157 lines = 52 × 3 + 1. The accession namespaces are also disjoint — CAID 3 targets occupy the higher `DP038xx`–`DP043xx` range, reflecting the newer ID space of the later experiment. Shipped prediction results for both challenges live in `reproduction/results/caid2/` and `reproduction/results/caid3/`, mirroring the benchmark split.

Sources: [data/README.md](data/README.md#L29-L36), [data/test/caid2_binding.fasta](data/test/caid2_binding.fasta#L1-L3), [data/test/caid3_binding.fasta](data/test/caid3_binding.fasta#L148-L157), [reproduction/README.md](reproduction/README.md#L5-L10)

The relationship between the three sets is a chain of increasing restriction — same record format, shrinking evaluation scope:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["CAID Web Portal<br/>(community benchmark source)"] --> B["caid2_binding.fasta<br/>CAID 2 Binding challenge<br/>78 targets · DP02342–DP03739"]
    A --> C["caid3_binding.fasta<br/>CAID 3 Binding challenge<br/>52 targets · DP03818–DP04391"]
    C -->|"same 52 sequences<br/>same binding labels"| D["caid3_binding_idr.fasta<br/>CAID 3 Binding-IDR challenge<br/>52 targets · non-IDR positions masked"]
    B -.->|"identical 3-line<br/>record format"| C
```

## Anatomy of a Benchmark Record

Every record in all three files is a fixed three-line block. Line 1 is the header (`>DP0xxxxx`, the CAID target accession). Line 2 is the full amino-acid sequence on a single line. Line 3 is a per-residue label string of exactly the same length as the sequence: `1` marks an experimentally annotated binding residue, `0` marks a non-binding residue, and (only in the Binding-IDR file) `-` marks a masked position. The evaluation parser in `table_1.py` consumes exactly this layout, taking line 2 as `aa` and mapping line 3 to an integer list as `label` — confirming that the label line is a first-class data field, not decoration.

| Line | Content | Example (from `DP03818`) |
|---|---|---|
| Header | `>` + CAID accession | `>DP03818` |
| Sequence | Single-line amino acids | `FVQWFSKFLGRIL` |
| Label | Position-aligned `0`/`1` (`-` = masked in Binding-IDR file) | `1111111111111` |

The example above is instructive because it is degenerate in a useful way: this 13-residue peptide is entirely disorder and entirely binding, so its label line is all `1`s in both CAID 3 files. At the other extreme, proteins like `DP03927` carry well-defined ordered domains with a single binding segment, and their label lines are mostly `0`s. This heterogeneity — short all-disordered peptides mixed with large multi-domain proteins — is characteristic of CAID target sets and is why per-residue metrics such as Fmax (rather than plain accuracy) dominate the evaluation.

Sources: [data/test/caid3_binding.fasta](data/test/caid3_binding.fasta#L1-L3), [data/test/caid2_binding.fasta](data/test/caid2_binding.fasta#L1-L6), [reproduction/scripts/table_1.py](reproduction/scripts/table_1.py#L29-L41)

## Binding vs. Binding-IDR: How the `-` Mask Restricts Evaluation

The two CAID 3 files contain byte-identical sequences and identical binding annotations — the *only* difference is that `caid3_binding_idr.fasta` replaces the label `0`/`1` with `-` at every position lying outside an annotated intrinsically disordered region (IDR). A masked position is excluded from scoring entirely; it is neither positive nor negative. This implements the premise of the Binding-IDR challenge: the model should be judged on whether it finds binding sites *within disordered context*, not penalized for (or credited with) behavior on structured segments.

Protein `DP03914` makes the semantics concrete. Its first 30 residues and everything after position ~66 are outside the annotated IDR, so in the IDR file those label positions become `-`, while the central binding segment `RREIESLIDSILSSSAG` (all `1`s) and its flanking disordered `0` residues survive. Note also that three proteins in the set (`DP03927`, `DP03930`, `DP03990`) are masked end-to-end in the IDR file — they carry no IDR annotation, so they contribute nothing to Binding-IDR scoring while remaining fully active in the plain Binding challenge.

| Segment of `DP03914` | Positions | Sequence | `caid3_binding` label | `caid3_binding_idr` label |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Outside annotated IDR | 0–29 | `MQARREELLAKKARLAEIKRQRELRAQQA` | `0…0` | `-…-` (masked) |
| Disordered, non-binding | 30–48 | `GRSITPSELVSPTPSRANS` | `0…0` | `0…0` |
| Disordered, binding | 49–65 | `RREIESLIDSILSSSAG` | `1…1` | `1…1` |
| Outside annotated IDR | 66–end | remainder of sequence | `0…0` | `-…-` (masked) |

Sources: [data/test/caid3_binding.fasta](data/test/caid3_binding.fasta#L4-L6), [data/test/caid3_binding_idr.fasta](data/test/caid3_binding_idr.fasta#L4-L15), [data/README.md](data/README.md#L31-L33)

> [!TIP]
> The `-` mask is a genuine third label value, not cosmetic formatting. When you build your own evaluation against `caid3_binding_idr.fasta`, a naive `int(char)` parse will crash on `-` and, worse, silently treating `-` as `0` would flood the negative class with hundreds of structured residues and deflate your metrics relative to the official CAID scoring.

## Evaluation Data Flow: From Benchmark Files to Manuscript Numbers

The benchmark files never touch the model directly — instead, they are paired with shipped prediction artifacts in `reproduction/results/`. Predictions for CAID targets are stored in the official CAID submission format (`.caid`): a `>DP0xxxxx` header followed by one tab-separated line per residue carrying the zero-based index, amino acid, predicted probability (six decimals), and a binary prediction derived from the model's decision threshold — the same threshold mechanism configured in [Inference Orchestration and Decision Threshold](10-inference-orchestration-and-decision-threshold). For CAID 3 there is additionally a per-protein CSV layer (`caid3/csv/DP0xxxxx.csv`) that merges, residue by residue, the benchmark ground truth with both the binding prediction and the auxiliary structural heads, including AlphaFold-derived reference columns (`af_plddt`, `af_rsa`, `af_ss8`) that are empty where no reference exists.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph GT["Ground truth (data/test)"]
        GT1["caid3_binding.fasta<br/>52 × (seq + 0/1 labels)"]
    end
    subgraph PRED["Shipped predictions (reproduction/results)"]
        P1["caid3_DARUMA-binding.caid<br/>CAID portal format:<br/>index · AA · prob · binary"]
        P2["caid3/csv/DP0xxxxx.csv<br/>ground truth + binding pred<br/>+ pLDDT/RSA/SS heads"]
    end
    GT1 -->|"align by accession"| S1["table_1.py<br/>AUC · APS · Fmax · coverage"]
    P1 --> S1
    P2 --> S2["table_2.py<br/>PCC/RMSE (pLDDT, RSA) · Q3/Q8 accuracy<br/>stratified by TP/FN/FP/TN"]
    P2 --> S3["table_3.py<br/>TPR · FPR · precision"]
```

Each reproduction script binds one benchmark set to one results directory: `table_1.py` loads the CAID 3 ground truth from `../../data/test/caid3_binding.fasta` and scores the `.caid` predictions against it; `table_2.py` and `table_3.py` glob the per-protein CSVs instead. All three scripts aggregate across proteins before computing metrics, which mirrors how CAID itself pools per-residue scores across the whole target set. The auxiliary-feature evaluation in `table_2.py` first applies a residue-level filter keeping only rows where `af_plddt` is non-empty — i.e., only positions with an AlphaFold reference are scored — and then partitions those residues into the four binding-confusion quadrants (TP/FN/FP/TN from the `y` vs. `db_preds` columns) to ask whether structural-head fidelity differs between correctly and incorrectly predicted binding residues.

| Script | Benchmark file consumed | Prediction artifact | Metrics computed |
|---|---|---|---|
| `table_1.py` | `data/test/caid3_binding.fasta` | `caid3_DARUMA-binding.caid` | AUC, APS, Fmax, coverage |
| `table_2.py` | (labels embedded in CSV) | `caid3/csv/*.csv` | PCC/RMSE for pLDDT & RSA, Q3/Q8 accuracy, per-quadrant breakdown |
| `table_3.py` | (labels embedded in CSV) | `caid3/csv/*.csv` | TPR, FPR, precision |

Sources: [reproduction/results/caid2/caid2_DARUMA-binding.caid](reproduction/results/caid2/caid2_DARUMA-binding.caid#L1-L8), [reproduction/results/caid3/csv/DP03818.csv](reproduction/results/caid3/csv/DP03818.csv#L1-L2), [reproduction/scripts/table_1.py](reproduction/scripts/table_1.py#L59-L74), [reproduction/scripts/table_2.py](reproduction/scripts/table_2.py#L57-L83), [reproduction/scripts/table_2.py](reproduction/scripts/table_2.py#L111-L115), [reproduction/scripts/table_3.py](reproduction/scripts/table_3.py#L42-L60)

> [!TIP]
> `table_1.py` computes coverage dynamically as `len(result_dict) / len(dataset_dict)` — the fraction of benchmark targets for which predictions exist — rather than assuming 1.0. This is the correct pattern for CAID-style evaluation because the community scoring pipeline allows partial submissions; if you regenerate predictions yourself and some targets fail, your coverage will diverge from the shipped run and headline AUC/APS figures are not directly comparable unless coverage matches.

## Critical Caveat: Benchmark Files Are Ground Truth, Not `predict.py` Input

The test FASTA files are a *superset* of FASTA, and this distinction matters operationally. The production reader in `backend/functions.py` treats everything after a header line as sequence: `read_fasta` splits records on `\n>` and then strips all newlines from the remainder. Fed `caid2_binding.fasta`, it would happily return the sequence with its entire `0`/`1` label string concatenated onto it — digits that are outside the amino-acid alphabet and would corrupt ProtT5 tokenization downstream. The three-line format is therefore parsed only by dedicated evaluation readers (`read_caid_dataset_file` in `table_1.py`), while `predict.py` is designed for plain FASTA like `examples/example.fasta`.

| Consumer | File type | Parse behavior |
|---|---|---|
| `src/daruma_binding/predict.py` → `read_fasta` | Plain FASTA (sequence only) | Header → accession; all remaining lines joined into sequence |
| `reproduction/scripts/table_1.py` → `read_caid_dataset_file` | 3-line benchmark record | Line 1 → accession, line 2 → `aa`, line 3 → integer label list |

If you want to score the benchmark sets with a fresh model run, strip line 3 (and, for the IDR file, decide your mask policy) before invoking `predict.py`, then align your probabilities back to the ground-truth label lines by accession exactly as `table_1.py` does. The detailed dataset-construction, redundancy-reduction, and splitting procedures are documented in the accompanying manuscript rather than in-code, per the data README.

Sources: [src/daruma_binding/backend/functions.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/functions.py#L12-L23), [src/daruma_binding/predict.py](src/daruma_binding/predict.py#L55-L73), [reproduction/scripts/table_1.py](reproduction/scripts/table_1.py#L29-L41), [data/README.md](data/README.md#L35-L37)

## Metrics Scored on These Sets (Primer)

Four numbers summarize the Binding challenge results: **AUC** (threshold-independent ranking quality over all residues), **APS** (area under the precision-recall curve, robust to the heavy class imbalance typical of binding annotations), **Fmax** (the maximum F-score swept over probability thresholds, the CAID convention for residue-level predictors), and **coverage** (fraction of targets predicted). Together they decouple three failure modes you can otherwise conflate: can the model rank binding residues high (AUC), does it concentrate precision where it matters (APS/Fmax), and did it run at all (coverage). The mathematical definitions, threshold-sweep mechanics, and imbalance behavior are treated fully in [Evaluation Metrics: AUC, APS, Fmax](14-evaluation-metrics-auc-aps-fmax); the step-by-step execution of the scoring scripts belongs to [Reproducing Paper Figures and Tables](13-reproducing-paper-figures-and-tables).

Sources: [reproduction/scripts/table_1.py](reproduction/scripts/table_1.py#L44-L74)

## Where to Go Next

A logical reading progression from here: learn how the model was fitted on complementary corpora in [Training Data and Zenodo Archive](12-training-data-and-zenodo-archive), then execute the scoring pipeline yourself with [Reproducing Paper Figures and Tables](13-reproducing-paper-figures-and-tables), ground the metric definitions in [Evaluation Metrics: AUC, APS, Fmax](14-evaluation-metrics-auc-aps-fmax), and finally explore the per-residue interpretability artifacts stored alongside the CAID 3 CSVs in [Occlusion-Based Feature Attribution](15-occlusion-based-feature-attribution). For the inference-side machinery that generated the `.caid` files being scored here — embedding chunking, thresholding, and output writing — see [ProtT5 Embedding Chunking Strategy](9-prott5-embedding-chunking-strategy) and [Inference Orchestration and Decision Threshold](10-inference-orchestration-and-decision-threshold).


# Training Data and Zenodo Archive



This page documents how DARUMA-binding's datasets are distributed across two locations: the GitHub repository (validation and benchmark data) and a Zenodo archive (the large training corpora). It specifies the on-disk record format, the label alphabet and its IDR-masking semantics, and the exact Zenodo identifiers needed to assemble a complete training environment.

## The Two-Tier Data Distribution Model

DARUMA-binding deliberately splits its data assets between the repository and Zenodo. The repository's `data/` directory carries everything needed for **evaluation and development sanity-checking** — the validation splits and the CAID benchmark test sets — while the large training corpora are archived separately on Zenodo. The repository README states this explicitly: `data/` contains "Validation and test datasets. Large training datasets are available separately from Zenodo" [README.md](README.md#L60-L66).

This split matters practically: the `data/README.md` documents **four** training files (`train_binding.txt`, `train_plddt.txt`, `train_rsa.txt`, `train_ss.txt`), yet only `train_binding.txt` actually exists in `data/training/`. The three auxiliary-feature training files are referenced in documentation but physically reside in the Zenodo archive — so reproducing training of the full model stack requires the archive download, not just the repository clone [data/README.md](data/README.md#L11-L20).

The following diagram shows the complete data landscape and how each compartment feeds the models:

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph ZEN["Zenodo Archive — DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24127965"]
        TP["train_plddt.txt"]
        TR["train_rsa.txt"]
        TS["train_ss.txt"]
    end

    subgraph REPO["Repository — data/"]
        subgraph TRAIN["training/"]
            TB["train_binding.txt<br/>3,145 records"]
        end
        subgraph VAL["validation/"]
            VB["val_binding.txt<br/>522 records"]
            VP["val_plddt.txt"]
            VR["val_rsa.txt"]
            VS["val_ss.txt"]
        end
        subgraph TEST["test/"]
            T2["caid2_binding.fasta"]
            T3["caid3_binding.fasta"]
            T3I["caid3_binding_idr.fasta"]
        end
    end

    MAIN["Binding Model<br/>(main predictor)"]
    DAF["DAF-pLDDT / DAF-RSA / DAF-SS<br/>(auxiliary feature models)"]

    TB --> MAIN
    VB --> MAIN
    TP -.-> DAF
    TR -.-> DAF
    TS -.-> DAF
    VP --> DAF
    VR --> DAF
    VS --> DAF
    T2 --> BENCH["CAID Benchmark<br/>Evaluation"]
    T3 --> BENCH
    T3I --> BENCH
```
