The auxiliary model mapping is documented per file: `val_plddt.txt`, `val_rsa.txt`, and `val_ss.txt` are explicitly labeled as validation data for the **DAF-pLDDT**, **DAF-RSA**, and **DAF-SS** models respectively — the auxiliary structural feature heads covered in [Auxiliary Structural Feature Heads](7-auxiliary-structural-feature-heads) [data/README.md](data/README.md#L22-L27).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L60-L66), [data/README.md](data/README.md#L11-L27)

## Repository Data Layout

The repository contains three data compartments, each in a fixed plain-text format:

| Path | Records* | Target Model | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| `data/training/train_binding.txt` | 3,145 | Main binding predictor | Training split (in repo) |
| `data/validation/val_binding.txt` | 522 | Main binding predictor | Validation split |
| `data/validation/val_plddt.txt` | — | DAF-pLDDT | Auxiliary-feature validation |
| `data/validation/val_rsa.txt` | — | DAF-RSA | Auxiliary-feature validation |
| `data/validation/val_ss.txt` | — | DAF-SS | Auxiliary-feature validation |
| `data/test/caid2_binding.fasta` | 78 | Benchmark evaluation | CAID 2 Binding challenge |
| `data/test/caid3_binding.fasta` | — | Benchmark evaluation | CAID 3 Binding challenge |
| `data/test/caid3_binding_idr.fasta` | — | Benchmark evaluation | CAID 3 Binding-IDR challenge |

\*Record counts are derived arithmetically from verified total line counts: each file holds 3-line records terminated by a single trailing blank line (`train_binding.txt`: 9,436 lines → (9436−1)/3 = 3,145; `val_binding.txt`: 1,567 lines → 522; `caid2_binding.fasta`: 235 lines → 78). The auxiliary validation files were confirmed present in `data/validation/` via directory inspection but are not human-readable through a line-based viewer.

Sources: [data/README.md](data/README.md#L7-L9), [data/training/train_binding.txt](data/training/train_binding.txt#L9430-L9436), [data/validation/val_binding.txt](data/validation/val_binding.txt#L1560-L1567), [data/test/caid2_binding.fasta](data/test/caid2_binding.fasta#L228-L235)

## Record Format Specification

All binding datasets share one **three-line-per-record** convention. A record consists of: (1) a FASTA-style header beginning with `>`, (2) the full amino-acid sequence on a single unwrapped line, and (3) a per-residue label line of identical length. For example, record `DP00003` in the training file spans three lines — header, sequence, and its label string [data/training/train_binding.txt](data/training/train_binding.txt#L1-L3).

The label line uses a three-symbol alphabet, not plain binary:

| Symbol | Meaning | Training Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `1` | Binding residue (within IDR) | Positive training signal |
| `0` | Non-binding residue (within IDR) | Negative training signal |
| `-` | Masked residue (outside annotated IDR) | Excluded from loss computation |

> [!TIP]
> The `-` character is the key to understanding label semantics: it aligns the label string with IDR annotations. Record `IID90024` in the validation split shows the canonical pattern — `-` runs across the ordered regions, while an internal disordered segment carries `000000001111111` before returning to `-`. Only residues inside annotated IDR segments receive binding labels; everything else is masked, which is exactly why the model's decision boundary is scoped to intrinsically disordered regions.

Two evidence-backed observations about the corpus composition: first, accession headers come from two families — early records use `DP` prefixes (`DP00003`, `DP00004`, `DP00005`), while later records use `IID` prefixes (`IID90015`, `IID90024`, `IID90042`), reflecting multiple source databases merged during corpus construction [data/validation/val_binding.txt](data/validation/val_binding.txt#L1560-L1567). Second, entire proteins can be uniformly labeled: `DP00005` is all-`1` (fully binding IDR) and `IID90044` is all-`0`, so the corpus includes both extremes rather than only mixed records [data/training/train_binding.txt](data/training/train_binding.txt#L4-L6).

> [!TIP]
> The test files carry a `.fasta` extension but are **not standard FASTA**: every record contains a third line of per-residue ground-truth labels (`0`/`1`) after the sequence line, as seen in `DP02342` of the CAID 2 file [data/test/caid2_binding.fasta](data/test/caid2_binding.fasta#L1-L6). Any parser written against standard FASTA conventions will misinterpret these files — treat the label line as a required third field of each record.

Sources: [data/training/train_binding.txt](data/training/train_binding.txt#L1-L12), [data/validation/val_binding.txt](data/validation/val_binding.txt#L1560-L1567), [data/test/caid2_binding.fasta](data/test/caid2_binding.fasta#L1-L6)

## The Zenodo Archive

Two distinct Zenodo records are associated with this project, and they serve different purposes:

| Resource | DOI | Contents |
|---|---|---|
| Training data archive | `10.5281/zenodo.24127965` | Large training datasets, including `train_plddt.txt`, `train_rsa.txt`, `train_ss.txt` |
| Manuscript version archive | `10.5281/zenodo.24133355` | Versioned snapshot of DARUMA-binding corresponding to the manuscript (for citation) |

The training archive is the authoritative source for the corpora the repository omits. The README's Data Availability section states: "The large training datasets used in this study are available from Zenodo," followed by the training-data DOI, with the note that "Validation and test datasets used for evaluation are included in this repository where applicable" [README.md](README.md#L76-L82). The same DOI is repeated in the `data/` README beside the list of training files [data/README.md](data/README.md#L18-L20).

The second DOI serves reproducibility governance rather than data transfer: "The version of DARUMA-binding corresponding to the manuscript is archived on Zenodo" at `10.5281/zenodo.24133355` [README.md](README.md#L109-L113). This is the reference you cite when your work depends on the exact manuscript-era code state, independent of any subsequent repository changes.

**Practical assembly path for full training reproduction**: clone the repository (gives you `train_binding.txt`, all validation files, and benchmark sets) + download the training archive at `10.5281/zenodo.24127965` (gives you the three auxiliary training files) → place the auxiliary files alongside `train_binding.txt` to reconstruct the complete four-file training corpus.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L76-L82), [README.md](README.md#L109-L113), [data/README.md](data/README.md#L18-L20)

## Provenance and Processing Boundaries

The benchmark test sets originate from the **CAID Web Portal**, with a one-to-one mapping documented in the data README: `caid2_binding.fasta` → CAID 2 Binding, `caid3_binding.fasta` → CAID 3 Binding, `caid3_binding_idr.fasta` → CAID 3 Binding-IDR [data/README.md](data/README.md#L29-L35). Their role in evaluation and scoring is covered in [CAID Benchmark Datasets](11-caid-benchmark-datasets) and [Evaluation Metrics: AUC, APS, Fmax](14-evaluation-metrics-auc-aps-fmax).

One scope boundary deserves emphasis: the repository documentation deliberately defers methodology to the manuscript. The data README closes with: "Detailed procedures for dataset construction, preprocessing, redundancy reduction, and dataset splitting are described in the associated manuscript" [data/README.md](data/README.md#L37). In other words, the repository documents *what* the data is and *where* it lives, but the *how* of redundancy reduction and train/validation/test partitioning is only verifiable in the paper — this documentation makes no claims about sequence identity thresholds or split construction beyond the splits' physical existence.

Sources: [data/README.md](data/README.md#L29-L37)

## Where to Go Next

With the data landscape mapped, the natural reading progression within this catalog is:

- [CAID Benchmark Datasets](11-caid-benchmark-datasets) — deep dive into the CAID 2/CAID 3 test sets introduced above, including challenge variants.
- [Auxiliary Structural Feature Heads](7-auxiliary-structural-feature-heads) — how the DAF-pLDDT/RSA/SS models consume the auxiliary feature files, which motivates the Zenodo-only training files.
- [Reproducing Paper Figures and Tables](13-reproducing-paper-figures-and-tables) — using the `reproduction/` scripts against the evaluation datasets in `data/test/`.
- [Evaluation Metrics: AUC, APS, Fmax](14-evaluation-metrics-auc-aps-fmax) — the metrics applied to those benchmark splits.


# Reproducing Paper Figures and Tables



The `reproduction/` directory is the empirical validation layer of the DARUMA-binding repository: it pairs **pre-computed prediction artifacts** with nine standalone Python scripts that regenerate every figure and table from the manuscript. Because all heavy model inference has already been done and its outputs are committed to the repository, you can verify the paper's reported metrics on a laptop in seconds — no GPU, no ProtT5, no model weights. Each script is deliberately flat and self-contained (parsing, metric computation, and plotting in one file) so that every number printed to your console is traceable to a specific file and code path. This page explains the artifact inventory, the three analysis families, the exact execution procedure, and the pitfalls that arise from the scripts' path conventions.

## Repository Layout: Artifacts vs. Scripts

The directory separates **results** (immutable data artifacts) from **scripts** (evaluation logic). The README states this contract explicitly: each script uses the corresponding files in the `results/` directory [README](reproduction/README.md#L1-L24).

| Path | Role | Contents |
|---|---|---|
| `reproduction/results/caid2/` | Benchmark predictions, CAID 2 | `caid2_DARUMA-binding.caid` (67,247 lines of per-residue scores) |
| `reproduction/results/caid3/` | Benchmark predictions, CAID 3 | `caid3_DARUMA-binding.caid` + a `csv/` folder of per-protein files |
| `reproduction/results/occlusion_analysis/` | Feature attribution data | 50 per-protein CSVs (`DP03818_occlusion.csv` … `DP04391_occlusion.csv`) |
| `reproduction/scripts/` | Evaluation scripts | 4 figure scripts + 5 table scripts |

The structure maps one-to-one onto the three analysis families: CAID benchmark scoring (`.caid` files), structural-feature agreement (`csv/`), and occlusion-based attribution (`occlusion_analysis/`). Note the symmetry: `figure_2.py`/`table_1.py` handle CAID 3 while their structural twins `figure_S1.py`/`table_S1.py` handle CAID 2 — the same code pattern applied to a different benchmark.

Sources: [README.md](reproduction/README.md#L5-L10), [caid2_DARUMA-binding.caid](reproduction/results/caid2/caid2_DARUMA-binding.caid#L1-L4)

## The Reproduction Workflow

Every script follows the same three-stage contract: **read artifact → align with ground truth → emit metric or plot**. The execution procedure is identical for all nine scripts.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["pip install -r requirements.txt"] --> B["cd reproduction/scripts"]
    B --> C{"Select analysis family"}
    C -->|"Benchmark scoring<br/>(.caid artifacts)"| D["table_1.py · table_S1.py · figure_2.py<br/>figure_S1.py · table_S2.py"]
    C -->|"Feature agreement<br/>(caid3/csv/*.csv)"| E["table_2.py · table_3.py"]
    C -->|"Occlusion attribution<br/>(occlusion_analysis/*.csv)"| F["figure_3.py · figure_4.py"]
    D --> G["Console metrics and/or<br/>interactive matplotlib window"]
    E --> G
    F --> G
```

> [!TIP]
> The single most important execution detail: **all scripts use relative paths and must be run from inside `reproduction/scripts/`**. They reference artifacts as `../results/...` and ground truth as `../../data/test/...` (e.g., `Path("../results/caid3").glob("*.caid")` in [figure_2.py](reproduction/scripts/figure_2.py#L68-L71)). Running from the repository root will silently glob zero files or fail with `FileNotFoundError`.

The dependency footprint is intentionally small — only three of the six root requirements matter here: `numpy`, `scikit-learn` (metrics), and `matplotlib` (plots) [requirements.txt](requirements.txt#L1-L6). Table scripts print text only; figure scripts call `plt.show()`, which opens an interactive window rather than saving image files, so run them in an environment with a display (or set a matplotlib backend).

Sources: [figure_2.py](reproduction/scripts/figure_2.py#L68-L87), [requirements.txt](requirements.txt#L1-L6)

## Script Inventory and Data Flow

Each script consumes a specific artifact family and aligns it against ground-truth labels. The alignment logic keys predictions to labels by **accession code (AC)** — the string after `>` in both files — then concatenates all residues across proteins into flat arrays for corpus-level scoring [figure_2.py](reproduction/scripts/figure_2.py#L73-L84).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Artifacts["reproduction/results/"]
        CAID2["caid2/*.caid"]
        CAID3["caid3/*.caid"]
        PERCSV["caid3/csv/*.csv<br/>(AF vs DARUMA features)"]
        OCC["occlusion_analysis/*.csv"]
    end
    subgraph Truth["data/test/ ground truth"]
        GT2["caid2_binding.fasta<br/>(binary 0/1)"]
        GT3["caid3_binding.fasta<br/>(binary 0/1)"]
        GTI["caid3_binding_idr.fasta<br/>(3-state -/0/1)"]
    end
    CAID2 --> FIGS1["figure_S1.py"] & TS1["table_S1.py"]
    CAID3 --> FIG2["figure_2.py"] & T1["table_1.py"]
    GT2 --> FIGS1 & TS1
    GT3 --> FIG2 & T1
    CAID3 --> T2["table_2.py"] & T3["table_3.py"]
    GTI --> TS2["table_S2.py"]
    CAID3 --> TS2
    OCC --> FIG3["figure_3.py"] & FIG4["figure_4.py"]
```

| Script | Artifact consumed | Ground truth | Output |
|---|---|---|---|
| `table_1.py` | `caid3/*.caid` | `caid3_binding.fasta` | AUC, APS, Fmax, Coverage |
| `table_S1.py` | `caid2/*.caid` | `caid2_binding.fasta` | AUC, APS, Fmax, Coverage |
| `table_S2.py` | `caid3/*.caid` | `caid3_binding_idr.fasta` | Same metrics, IDR-masked |
| `figure_2.py` | `caid3/*.caid` | `caid3_binding.fasta` | ROC + PR curves |
| `figure_S1.py` | `caid2/*.caid` | `caid2_binding.fasta` | ROC + PR curves |
| `table_2.py` | `caid3/csv/*.csv` | labels + AF features in CSV | PCC/RMSE/Q8/Q3, confusion-stratified |
| `table_3.py` | `caid3/csv/*.csv` | labels + AF features in CSV | TPR/FPR/Precision per AF quadrant |
| `figure_3.py` | `occlusion_analysis/*.csv` | self-contained | ROC curves + ΔAUC per feature |
| `figure_4.py` | `occlusion_analysis/*.csv` | self-contained | Δ-probability violin plots |

Sources: [README.md](reproduction/README.md#L12-L24), [figure_2.py](reproduction/scripts/figure_2.py#L73-L84)

## Input Artifact Formats

The three artifact families use distinct formats. Understanding them is prerequisite to interpreting or extending any script.

**CAID format** (`.caid`): comment lines starting with `#` are skipped; each protein begins with `>AC`; every subsequent line is tab-separated `index<TAB>amino_acid<TAB>probability<TAB>binary_prediction` [caid2_DARUMA-binding.caid](reproduction/results/caid2/caid2_DARUMA-binding.caid#L1-L4). The parser collects these into a dict keyed by AC with `probability` (float) and `binary_prediction` (int) lists [figure_2.py](reproduction/scripts/figure_2.py#L9-L27).

**Ground-truth FASTA**: a three-line block convention — `>AC`, then the sequence, then a label string of equal length where each character is a residue label (e.g., `DP03818` / `FVQWFSKFLGRIL` / `1111111111111`) [caid3_binding.fasta](data/test/caid3_binding.fasta#L1-L6). `table_S2.py` extends this to three states, mapping `-` to −1 (ignore), `0`, and `1`, which is the CAID 3 IDR-restricted evaluation [table_S2.py](reproduction/scripts/table_S2.py#L30-L43).

**Per-protein CSV** (`caid3/csv/`): a header plus one row per residue with ten columns comparing AlphaFold-derived reference features (`af_plddt`, `af_rsa`, `af_ss8` — empty where reference data is unavailable) against DARUMA-binding's auxiliary head outputs (`db_preds`, `db_plddt`, `db_rsa`, `db_ss3`, `db_ss8`) [DP03818.csv](reproduction/results/caid3/csv/DP03818.csv#L1-L6).

**Occlusion CSV** (`occlusion_analysis/`): per-residue rows with the ground-truth label `y`, the model's `original_probs`, and five re-prediction columns where each auxiliary input was occluded in turn (`plddt_occluded_probs`, `rsa_occluded_probs`, `helix/sheet/coil_occluded_probs`) [figure_3.py](reproduction/scripts/figure_3.py#L9-L35).

| Format | Delimiter | Key columns | Used by |
|---|---|---|---|
| CAID | tab | probability, binary_prediction | table_1/S1/S2, figure_2/S1 |
| Ground-truth FASTA | 3-line blocks | label string per residue | table_1/S1/S2, figure_2/S1 |
| Per-protein CSV | comma | af_* vs db_* feature pairs | table_2, table_3 |
| Occlusion CSV | comma | original vs 5 occluded prob columns | figure_3, figure_4 |

Sources: [DP03818.csv](reproduction/results/caid3/csv/DP03818.csv#L1-L6), [caid3_binding.fasta](data/test/caid3_binding.fasta#L1-L6)

## Family 1: Benchmark Scoring (Tables 1, S1, S2; Figures 2, S1)

The table scripts compute the four headline metrics — AUC via `roc_auc_score`, APS via `average_precision_score`, Fmax via a precision–recall sweep, and Coverage as the fraction of dataset proteins that received predictions [table_1.py](reproduction/scripts/table_1.py#L59-L74). The Fmax implementation scans `sklearn`'s `precision_recall_curve` output, guards the F-score denominator with a `1e-8` epsilon, and also returns the threshold that achieves the maximum [table_1.py](reproduction/scripts/table_1.py#L44-L49) — these are the exact metrics formalized in [Evaluation Metrics: AUC, APS, Fmax](14-evaluation-metrics-auc-aps-fmax).

`table_S2.py` is the subtle variant: because `caid3_binding_idr.fasta` uses three-state labels, it masks out every residue labeled `-` before pooling, so scoring is restricted to residues with confident ground truth [table_S2.py](reproduction/scripts/table_S2.py#L66-L73). This reproduces the manuscript's IDR-restricted CAID 3 comparison and complements the dataset definitions in [CAID Benchmark Datasets](11-caid-benchmark-datasets).

The figure scripts reuse identical parsing but render curves instead: `figure_2.py` plots ROC (with the diagonal chance line) and precision–recall curves for every `*.caid` file in `results/caid3/` [figure_2.py](reproduction/scripts/figure_2.py#L45-L65), while `figure_S1.py` performs the same on `results/caid2/` against `caid2_binding.fasta` [figure_S1.py](reproduction/scripts/figure_S1.py#L68-L87). Because they glob rather than hard-code filenames, dropping additional `.caid` files into the results folders automatically adds competitor curves.

## Family 2: Structural Feature Agreement (Tables 2, 3)

`table_2.py` quantifies how faithfully DARUMA-binding's auxiliary heads reproduce their AlphaFold-derived training targets. Part (a) pools all residues with available reference data and reports **PCC and RMSE** for pLDDT and RSA, plus 8-class (Q8) and 3-class (Q3) accuracy for secondary structure — the latter via an explicit Q8→Q3 collapse table (`H/G/I→H`, `E/B→S`, `T/S/C→C`) [table_2.py](reproduction/scripts/table_2.py#L85-L108). Part (b) repeats the same statistics stratified by the TP/FN/FP/TN confusion classes of the binding prediction [table_2.py](reproduction/scripts/table_2.py#L111-L128), revealing whether feature fidelity differs where the model is right versus wrong.

> [!TIP]
> Scripts `table_2.py` and `table_3.py` filter rows with `mask = np.array(full_result_dict["af_plddt"]) != None` before any comparison [table_2.py](reproduction/scripts/table_2.py#L81-L83). This relies on element-wise `!=` against `None` producing a boolean array under NumPy — residues without AlphaFold reference data are silently excluded, which is why their reported `n` counts are smaller than the raw residue totals.

`table_3.py` asks a different question: where does prediction quality concentrate relative to structural confidence? It thresholds reference features at **pLDDT > 70** and **RSA > 0.25** to define four quadrants — HH, HL, LH, LL — then reports residue counts, binding-residue counts, TPR, FPR, and Precision per quadrant [table_3.py](reproduction/scripts/table_3.py#L86-L100). The metric helpers here are hand-rolled from confusion counts rather than scikit-learn calls [table_3.py](reproduction/scripts/table_3.py#L42-L55), making the per-quadrant arithmetic directly inspectable.

## Family 3: Occlusion-Based Attribution (Figures 3, 4)

These scripts consume the 50 occlusion CSVs and require no external ground truth — each row carries its own label `y`. `figure_3.py` pools all proteins, plots one ROC curve per condition (original plus five occluded variants), then prints each feature's occluded AUC alongside the **delta AUC** against the original — a negative delta quantifies how much that auxiliary input contributes to binding discrimination [figure_3.py](reproduction/scripts/figure_3.py#L71-L88). The occlusion procedure that generated these files is described in [Occlusion-Based Feature Attribution](15-occlusion-based-feature-attribution).

`figure_4.py` transforms the same data into per-residue **Δ-probability distributions** (`original − occluded`) and renders violin plots with mean markers, first across all residues and then stratified by confusion class [figure_4.py](reproduction/scripts/figure_4.py#L80-L151). The stratification uses a hard-coded decision threshold of **0.26** to define TP/FN/FP/TN masks [figure_4.py](reproduction/scripts/figure_4.py#L100-L103) — this is the same deployment threshold derived and documented in [Inference Orchestration and Decision Threshold](10-inference-orchestration-and-decision-threshold), so any change to that threshold must be mirrored here for the figure to remain consistent with the manuscript.

## Common Pitfalls and Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `FileNotFoundError` on a `.caid` or `.fasta` path | Script run from repo root or elsewhere | `cd reproduction/scripts` first; all paths are relative to it |
| Figure script prints nothing / plots no curves | Glob matched zero files (wrong CWD, or results folder missing) | Verify `../results/...` resolves from your working directory |
| `plt.show()` hangs or errors on a headless server | Interactive backend with no display | Use `matplotlib.use("Agg")` + `plt.savefig(...)`, or run locally with X forwarding |
| `table_S2` scores differ from `table_1` on CAID 3 | Expected: S2 masks `-`-labeled IDR positions before pooling | Compare only against the manuscript's IDR-restricted table |
| Reproduced metrics deviate slightly | scikit-learn version drift affects `roc_curve`/`precision_recall_curve` tie handling | Pin the root `requirements.txt` versions (`scikit-learn==1.7.2`, `numpy==1.26.4`) |
| Figure 4 quadrant counts look small | Residues without AF reference data are masked out | This is intentional filtering of `af_plddt == None` rows |

Sources: [requirements.txt](requirements.txt#L1-L6), [table_S2.py](reproduction/scripts/table_S2.py#L66-L73)

## Where to Go Next

To understand *how* the `.caid` artifacts were produced — the model, the ProtT5 embedding pipeline, and the argmax/binary-threshold output stages these scripts decode — continue to [Prediction Pipeline Architecture](5-prediction-pipeline-architecture) and [Inference Orchestration and Decision Threshold](10-inference-orchestration-and-decision-threshold). For the construction and composition of the two benchmarks being scored here, see [CAID Benchmark Datasets](11-caid-benchmark-datasets); the formal definitions of AUC, APS, and the Fmax sweep appear in [Evaluation Metrics: AUC, APS, Fmax](14-evaluation-metrics-auc-aps-fmax). If you want to regenerate the occlusion artifacts themselves rather than only their figures, [Occlusion-Based Feature Attribution](15-occlusion-based-feature-attribution) covers the generation procedure that `figure_3.py` and `figure_4.py` visualize.


# Evaluation Metrics: AUC, APS, Fmax



This page explains how DARUMA-binding is quantitatively evaluated. The repository does not ship metrics inside the inference package — all three headline metrics (AUC, APS, Fmax) are implemented in the `reproduction/scripts/` layer, where paper tables and figures are reproduced from archived prediction files. Here we trace the full path from CAID-format prediction files and ground-truth datasets to the final numbers, explain the mathematical definition and exact implementation of each metric, and document the benchmark variants (CAID 2, CAID 3, and the IDR-restricted subset) that share this machinery.

Sources: [README.md](/reproduction/README.md#L1-L24), [table_1.py](/reproduction/scripts/table_1.py#L44-L56)

## Where Metrics Live: The Reproduction Layer

A key architectural fact: neither the standalone predictor (`src/daruma_binding/`) nor the CAID submission package (`caid/DARUMA-binding/`) contains any evaluation code — the CAID package's `utils.py` is limited to FASTA parsing. Metric computation is deliberately isolated in the reproduction scripts, keeping inference and evaluation decoupled. Each script is self-contained: it embeds its own file parsers and metric helpers rather than importing from a shared metrics module, so the three table scripts (`table_1.py`, `table_S1.py`, `table_S2.py`) carry byte-identical copies of `calculate_fmax` and `calculate_metrics`. This duplication is intentional for reproducibility — every paper artifact can be regenerated from a single file.

The metric implementations and their consumers break down as follows:

| Script | Metrics computed | sklearn functions | Consumes | Benchmark |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `table_1.py` | AUC, APS, Fmax, Coverage | `roc_auc_score`, `average_precision_score`, `precision_recall_curve` | CAID3 `.caid` results | CAID 3 test set |
| `table_S1.py` | AUC, APS, Fmax, Coverage | same trio | CAID2 `.caid` results | CAID 2 test set |
| `table_S2.py` | AUC, APS, Fmax, Coverage (IDR subset) | same trio | CAID3 `.caid` results + IDR labels | CAID 3 IDR-only |
| `figure_2.py` / `figure_S1.py` | ROC curves, PR curves | `roc_curve`, `precision_recall_curve` | all `*.caid` files in results dir | CAID 3 / CAID 2 |
| `figure_3.py` | AUC + ΔAUC per occluded variant | `roc_auc_score` | occlusion analysis CSVs | CAID 3 (attribution) |
| `table_2.py` / `table_3.py` | PCC, RMSE, accuracy, TPR/FPR/Precision | manual numpy | per-protein CSVs | auxiliary features & operating regions |

The row for `table_2.py` (structural-feature agreement metrics) and `table_3.py` (fixed-threshold confusion-region analysis) belongs to the auxiliary heads and threshold topics covered in [Auxiliary Structural Feature Heads](7-auxiliary-structural-feature-heads) and [Inference Orchestration and Decision Threshold](10-inference-orchestration-and-decision-threshold); this page focuses on the threshold-free metrics of the first five rows.

Sources: [table_1.py](/reproduction/scripts/table_1.py#L1-L75), [utils.py](/caid/DARUMA-binding/daruma_binding/utils/utils.py#L1-L16), [table_S1.py](/reproduction/scripts/table_S1.py#L44-L56), [table_S2.py](/reproduction/scripts/table_S2.py#L47-L59)

## From Prediction Files to Pooled Scores

Every metric script follows the same three-stage pipeline: **parse → pool → score**. Two parsers establish the data contract. `read_caid_result_file` reads the CAID submission format: lines beginning with `>` start a new accession, comment lines starting with `#` are skipped, and each residue is a tab-separated quadruple of residue index, amino acid, probability, and binary prediction. `read_caid_dataset_file` reads the ground-truth FASTA, where each protein occupies three lines — header, sequence, and a per-residue binary label string.

A concrete example from the CAID 3 ground truth shows the format: protein `DP03818` is a 13-residue peptide whose label line `1111111111111` marks every residue as binding:

```
>DP03818
FVQWFSKFLGRIL
1111111111111
```

The critical evaluation decision happens in the pooling stage. Residues from *all* proteins are concatenated into a single flat array before scoring (`full_probabilities.extend(...)` / `full_labels.extend(...)`), so AUC, APS, and Fmax are computed as **global residue-level (micro-averaged) metrics**, not averages of per-protein scores. A protein with 300 residues contributes 300 data points; a 13-residue peptide contributes 13. Coverage is reported alongside as a separate, non-threshold statistic — the fraction of proteins in the dataset for which the predictor produced output (`len(result_dict) / len(dataset_dict)`).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Inputs["Input artifacts"]
        A["CAID result files<br/>reproduction/results/*/**.caid"]
        B["Ground truth<br/>data/test/*.fasta"]
    end
    subgraph Parse["Embedded parsers"]
        C["read_caid_result_file<br/>(ac → probs, binary)"]
        D["read_caid_dataset_file<br/>(ac → aa, labels)"]
    end
    E["Global residue pooling<br/>extend() across all proteins"]
    F["calculate_metrics"]
    G1["roc_auc_score → AUC"]
    G2["average_precision_score → APS"]
    G3["calculate_fmax → Fmax"]
    H["Console report<br/>AUC / APS / Fmax / Coverage"]
    A --> C --> E
    B --> D --> E
    E --> F
    F --> G1
    F --> G2
    F --> G3
    G1 & G2 & G3 --> H
```

Sources: [table_1.py](/reproduction/scripts/table_1.py#L8-L41), [caid3_binding.fasta](/data/test/caid3_binding.fasta#L1-L6), [table_1.py](/reproduction/scripts/table_1.py#L59-L74)

## The Three Metrics: Definition and Implementation

All three metrics are **threshold-free**: they evaluate the ranking quality of the raw probabilities rather than the binary predictions. This is why the metric scripts read the `probability` column of the CAID files and ignore `binary_prediction` entirely.

| Metric | Conceptual definition | Implementation | Interpretation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **AUC** | Area under the ROC curve (TPR vs. FPR swept over all thresholds); probability that a random binding residue outranks a random non-binding one | `roc_auc_score(labels, probabilities)` | Ranking quality; insensitive to class imbalance |
| **APS** | Average precision — area under the precision-recall curve, computed as the precision-weighted sum over recall increments | `average_precision_score(labels, probabilities)` | Ranking quality under imbalance; stricter baseline = positive rate |
| **Fmax** | Maximum F1 score over *all* possible thresholds: `max_t 2·P(t)·R(t) / (P(t)+R(t))` | `calculate_fmax` via `precision_recall_curve` | Best achievable operating point, post-hoc |
| Coverage | Fraction of proteins with predictions | `len(result_dict) / len(dataset_dict)` | Completeness of submission |

The canonical implementation, identical in all three table scripts, is compact:

```python
def calculate_fmax(all_labels, all_probs):
    precision, recall, thresholds = precision_recall_curve(all_labels, all_probs)
    f_scores = 2 * (precision * recall) / (precision + recall + 1e-8)
    fmax = np.max(f_scores)
    best_threshold = thresholds[np.argmax(f_scores)] if len(thresholds) > 0 else 0.5
    return fmax, best_threshold

def calculate_metrics(probabilities, labels):
    auc = roc_auc_score(labels, probabilities)
    aps = average_precision_score(labels, probabilities)
    fmax = calculate_fmax(labels, probabilities)[0]
    return auc, aps, fmax
```

> [!TIP]
> The `+ 1e-8` epsilon in the F-score denominator is what lets Fmax survive the sentinel point that sklearn appends to `precision_recall_curve` output (precision = 1, recall = 0, one element longer than `thresholds`). At that sentinel the F-score collapses to ≈ `2·1·0 / (1+0+1e-8) ≈ 0`, so `np.argmax` can never spuriously select it — the epsilon is both a division-by-zero guard and an implicit sentinel suppressor.

Sources: [table_1.py](/reproduction/scripts/table_1.py#L44-L56), [table_S1.py](/reproduction/scripts/table_S1.py#L44-L56), [table_S2.py](/reproduction/scripts/table_S2.py#L47-L59)

## Fmax and the Decision Threshold: Benchmark to Inference

`calculate_fmax` returns two values, and the second one matters beyond the benchmark. The `best_threshold` — the probability cutoff at which F1 peaks on the evaluation set — is the *empirical* counterpart of the *fixed* operating threshold the predictor ships with. At inference time, the model binarizes probabilities with a hardcoded threshold of **0.26** (`pred = (prob > self.threshold).astype(int)` in `predict_from_x`), a value documented in the main README and reused throughout reproduction scripts.

The relationship forms a deliberate design loop:

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    P["precision_recall_curve(labels, probs)"] --> Q["precision / recall / thresholds arrays"]
    Q --> S["F-scores: 2PR / (P + R + 1e-8)"]
    S --> M["Fmax = max(F-scores) — reported in tables"]
    S --> T["best_threshold = thresholds[argmax(F)]"]
    T -. "benchmark-informed operating point" .-> O["Fixed inference threshold = 0.26<br/>models.py predict_from_x"]
    O --> W["figure_4.py: TP/FN/FP/TN masks<br/>(prob >= 0.26 vs. < 0.26)"]
    O --> X["predict.py ResultWriter<br/>binary column in output files"]
```

In other words, Fmax answers "how good could the operating point be?", while the shipped 0.26 threshold answers "how good is the deployed one?". The reproduction layer evaluates both worlds: the table scripts score threshold-free metrics, while `figure_4.py` slices occlusion deltas by the 0.26 boundary into TP/FN/FP/TN regions — linking attribution analysis directly to the deployed confusion matrix.

Sources: [table_1.py](/reproduction/scripts/table_1.py#L44-L49), [models.py](/src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L222-L240), [README.md](/README.md#L47-L57), [figure_4.py](/reproduction/scripts/figure_4.py#L100-L103), [predict.py](/src/daruma_binding/predict.py#L63-L71)

## Benchmark Variants: CAID 3, CAID 2, and the IDR Subset

The same metric core serves three evaluation contexts, differing only in inputs and one preprocessing step:

| Variant | Script | Result file | Ground truth | Special handling |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CAID 3, all residues | `table_1.py` | `results/caid3/caid3_DARUMA-binding.caid` | `data/test/caid3_binding.fasta` | none — all residues are labeled 0/1 |
| CAID 2, all residues | `table_S1.py` | `results/caid2/caid2_DARUMA-binding.caid` | `data/test/caid2_binding.fasta` | identical logic to `table_1.py` |
| CAID 3, IDR-only | `table_S2.py` | `results/caid3/caid3_DARUMA-binding.caid` | `data/test/caid3_binding_idr.fasta` | masks residues labeled `-1` before scoring |

The IDR variant is the only one requiring metric-relevant preprocessing. Its ground-truth reader maps labels through `{"-": -1, "0": 0, "1": 1}`, allowing three states; residues marked `-1` are excluded from the evaluation entirely by a boolean mask applied per protein before pooling:

```python
for ac in result_dict:
    mask = np.array(dataset_dict[ac]["label"]) != -1
    probabilities = np.array(result_dict[ac]["probability"])[mask]
    labels = np.array(dataset_dict[ac]["label"])[mask]
    full_probabilities.extend(probabilities)
    full_labels.extend(labels)
```

This is the correct way to handle unlabeled/ambiguous regions: excluded residues contribute to neither the numerator nor denominator of any metric, whereas feeding `-1` into `roc_auc_score` would either crash or silently distort the scores. Coverage here still uses raw protein counts, since it measures predictor completeness, not residue-level agreement.

Sources: [table_1.py](/reproduction/scripts/table_1.py#L59-L74), [table_S1.py](/reproduction/scripts/table_S1.py#L59-L74), [table_S2.py](/reproduction/scripts/table_S2.py#L30-L43), [table_S2.py](/reproduction/scripts/table_S2.py#L62-L77)

## Curve-Level Reproduction: ROC, PR, and AUC Deltas

Beyond scalar scores, two scripts render the curves from which AUC and APS are derived. `figure_2.py` (CAID 3) and `figure_S1.py` (CAID 2) share identical logic: they glob **every** `*.caid` file in the results directory, pool each one's probabilities against the same ground truth, and overlay one ROC curve and one precision-recall curve per file. The design is a comparison harness — the repository archives only `caid3_DARUMA-binding.caid`, but dropping additional methods' `.caid` files into `results/caid3/` plots them against DARUMA-binding with no code changes. The ROC helper also draws the diagonal chance line (`plt.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], "--")`) as a reference.

`figure_3.py` applies AUC as a *difference* instrument for feature attribution: it loads the occlusion-analysis CSVs, scores `roc_auc_score` for the original probabilities and for each feature-occluded variant, and reports `delta AUC = original_auc - occluded_auc` per feature. The magnitude of the drop quantifies how much each structural feature (pLDDT, RSA, helix, sheet, coil) contributes to binding ranking — the scalar-score counterpart to the curve work covered in [Occlusion-Based Feature Attribution](15-occlusion-based-feature-attribution).

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Scalar["Scalar metrics (tables)"]
        direction LR
        S1["Pooled probs + labels"] --> S2["roc_auc_score<br/>average_precision_score<br/>calculate_fmax"]
        S2 --> S3["AUC, APS, Fmax, Coverage"]
    end
    subgraph Curves["Curve metrics (figures)"]
        direction LR
        C1["roc_curve / precision_recall_curve<br/>per method (*.caid glob)"] --> C2["Overlaid ROC + PR plots<br/>figure_2, figure_S1"]
    end
    subgraph Delta["AUC as attribution signal"]
        direction LR
        D1["original probs vs. occluded probs"] --> D2["ΔAUC per feature<br/>figure_3"]
    end
    Scalar -. "same underlying (y_true, y_score)" .- Curves
    Curves -. "area under plotted curves = AUC / APS" .- Scalar
    Scalar --> Delta
```

Sources: [figure_2.py](/reproduction/scripts/figure_2.py#L45-L87), [figure_S1.py](/reproduction/scripts/figure_S1.py#L45-L87), [figure_3.py](/reproduction/scripts/figure_3.py#L79-L89), [README.md](/reproduction/README.md#L5-L10)

## Running the Evaluations Yourself

Each script runs standalone from the `reproduction/scripts/` directory and prints its metrics to stdout — no arguments, no configuration. The critical constraint is the **working directory**: all paths are relative (`../results/...`, `../../data/...`), so launching from the repo root will raise `FileNotFoundError`.

| Step | Command (from `reproduction/scripts/`) | Output | Dependencies |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CAID 3 headline scores | `python table_1.py` | AUC / APS / Fmax / Coverage, 4-decimal floats | numpy, scikit-learn |
| CAID 2 headline scores | `python table_S1.py` | same four numbers | numpy, scikit-learn |
| CAID 3 IDR-only scores | `python table_S2.py` | same four numbers on `-1`-masked labels | numpy, scikit-learn |
| CAID 3 curves | `python figure_2.py` | ROC + PR windows (one line per `.caid` file) | numpy, scikit-learn, matplotlib |
| CAID 2 curves | `python figure_S1.py` | ROC + PR windows | numpy, scikit-learn, matplotlib |
| Attribution ΔAUC | `python figure_3.py` | AUC and ΔAUC per occluded feature | numpy, scikit-learn |

The archived artifacts are complete — `results/caid2/caid2_DARUMA-binding.caid`, `results/caid3/caid3_DARUMA-binding.caid` plus 50 per-protein CSVs, and 50 occlusion CSVs — so every metric reported in the manuscript can be regenerated without rerunning the model. When verifying a reproduction, compare your console output digit-for-digit against the paper's Table 1/S1/S2 values; the metric functions are deterministic given identical input files.

> [!TIP]
> If you adapt these metrics to your own predictor, reuse the exact `calculate_fmax` implementation (epsilon and all) rather than substituting `f1_score` from sklearn — the epsilon changes the numerics at the fourth decimal place, which is the same precision at which the paper reports (`{:.4f}`), so a mismatch is visible and breaks comparability with published numbers.

Sources: [table_1.py](/reproduction/scripts/table_1.py#L59-L75), [table_S2.py](/reproduction/scripts/table_S2.py#L62-L85), [figure_2.py](/reproduction/scripts/figure_2.py#L68-L88), [README.md](/reproduction/README.md#L12-L24)

## Summary and Reading Path

Three principles summarize this evaluation layer. First, **metrics live apart from inference**: the predictor emits probabilities and a fixed-threshold binary column; scoring happens exclusively in `reproduction/scripts/`. Second, **threshold-free metrics dominate**: AUC, APS, and Fmax all rank raw probabilities over globally pooled residues, with Fmax additionally exposing the optimal threshold that contextualizes the shipped 0.26 cutoff. Third, **one metric core, three contexts**: identical functions evaluate CAID 3, CAID 2, and the IDR subset, with only label masking (`-1` exclusion) varying between them.

To continue through this catalog in dependency order: the datasets these metrics score are described in [CAID Benchmark Datasets](11-caid-benchmark-datasets) and [Training Data and Zenodo Archive](12-training-data-and-zenodo-archive), the mechanics of reproducing full figures and tables are in [Reproducing Paper Figures and Tables](13-reproducing-paper-figures-and-tables), the threshold that Fmax contextualizes is detailed in [Inference Orchestration and Decision Threshold](10-inference-orchestration-and-decision-threshold), and the ΔAUC attribution methodology previewed here is fully developed in [Occlusion-Based Feature Attribution](15-occlusion-based-feature-attribution).


# Occlusion-Based Feature Attribution



This page explains how DARUMA-binding quantifies *which predicted structural features actually drive its binding predictions* through an occlusion analysis. Rather than attributing importance to input residues (as saliency methods do), the analysis removes entire groups of predicted structural signals — pLDDT, RSA, and secondary-structure classes — and measures how the binding probability reacts. The repository ships the resulting per-protein artifacts under `reproduction/results/occlusion_analysis/` together with the two scripts (`figure_3.py`, `figure_4.py`) that turn them into manuscript Figures 3 and 4.

Sources: [reproduction/README.md](reproduction/README.md#L1-L24), [figure_3.py](reproduction/scripts/figure_3.py#L1-L8), [figure_4.py](reproduction/scripts/figure_4.py#L1-L3)

## Why Occlusion Fits This Architecture: A Clean Causal Probe

Occlusion is an intervention-based attribution method: a candidate information source is removed, the model is re-run, and the change in output is credited to that source. In most architectures this is messy — masking part of the input perturbs every downstream computation at once. DARUMA-binding's architecture makes the intervention unusually clean, because the binding head never sees the raw ProtT5 embedding. The three auxiliary structural heads (DAF-pLDDT, DAF-RSA, DAF-SS8) run inside a `torch.no_grad()` block, their softmax outputs are concatenated into a 12-channel tensor, and the multi-kernel convolution binding head consumes *only* that tensor:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    E["ProtT5 embedding<br/>(1, 1024, L)"] --> H1["DAF-pLDDT head"]
    E --> H2["DAF-RSA head"]
    E --> H3["DAF-SS8 head"]
    subgraph frozen["auxiliary feature extractor (under torch.no_grad)"]
        H1 --> F1[("pLDDT channels 0–1")]
        H2 --> F2[("RSA channels 2–3")]
        H3 --> F3[("SS8 channels 4–11")]
    end
    F1 --> X
    F2 --> X
    F3 --> X["feature tensor (1, L, 12)"]
    X -- "occlude one group" --> MK["Multi-kernel conv binding head<br/>(kernels 3, 7, 15, 31, 63, 127)"]
    MK --> P["binding probability"]
    P --> D["Δp = p_original − p_occluded<br/>per residue, per group"]
```

Because the features are computed with `torch.no_grad()` and then `detach().requires_grad_(True)` before entering the binding head, they act as frozen constants from the binding head's perspective. An occlusion experiment therefore modifies a genuine input of the binding head — not a gradient artifact — making the resulting Δp a direct causal measure of each feature group's contribution at every residue. This is also why the analysis targets *feature groups* rather than residues: the 12-channel tensor is the only interface through which structural information reaches the binding decision.

Sources: [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L175-L188), [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L137-L153), [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L157-L166)

> [!TIP]
> The `no_grad()` + `detach()` boundary at models.py#L176-L181 is what makes occlusion here well-defined: interventions on the 12-channel tensor cannot back-propagate into the auxiliary heads or ProtT5, and with `dropout_rate=0` the frozen heads are deterministic — so any probability change measured after occlusion is attributable solely to the masked channels.

## The Five Occlusion Targets over Twelve Channels

The channel vocabulary is declared explicitly in the model as `af_list`, and the SS3 collapse in `predict_from_x` confirms how the 8-state channels group into helix/sheet/coil. The occlusion study covers exactly five groups — one per structural concept — rather than all 12 channels individually:

| Occlusion group | Channels (index: semantic name) | Structural meaning | Equivalent SS3 view | Code evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **pLDDT** | 0: `plddt`, 1: `1-plddt` | per-residue structural confidence | — | softmax output of DAF-pLDDT |
| **RSA** | 2: `1-rsa`, 3: `rsa` | relative solvent accessibility | — | softmax output of DAF-RSA |
| **Helix** | 4: `ss0(Alphahelix)`, 5: `ss1(Helix_3)`, 6: `ss2(Helix_5)` | helical structure | SS3 `H` | `af_feature[..., 4:7].sum(-1)` |
| **Sheet** | 7: `ss3(Strand)`, 8: `ss4(BetaBridge)` | extended/β structure | SS3 `S` | `af_feature[..., 7:9].sum(-1)` |
| **Coil** | 9: `ss5(Turn)`, 10: `ss6(Bend)`, 11: `ss7(other)` | non-regular structure | SS3 `C` | `af_feature[..., 9:12].sum(-1)` |

Note that the Helix/Sheet/Coil groupings mirror the q8→q3 reduction the model itself performs when writing SS3 output (`H`/`G`/`I` → helix; `E`/`B` → sheet; `T`/`S`/`-` → coil), so the attribution is expressed in the same terms as the model's human-readable structural outputs.

Sources: [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L171-L172), [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L231-L238), [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L205-L220)

## The Occlusion Artifacts: 51 Per-Protein CSV Files

The intervention results are stored as one CSV per protein — 51 files named `DP03818_occlusion.csv` through `DP04391_occlusion.csv`. The `DP`-prefixed accessions identify proteins from the CAID3 Binding challenge test set: `DP03818` is the first entry of `data/test/caid3_binding.fasta`, and its 13 residues (`FVQWFSKFLGRIL`, all labeled binding) match the CSV rows one-to-one, including the per-residue ground-truth label `y`. Each file records, for every residue, the baseline probability plus one probability per occluded feature group:

| Column | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `residue` | single-letter string | amino acid at the position |
| `y` | int (0/1) | ground-truth binding annotation from CAID3 |
| `original_probs` | float | baseline binding probability, all 12 channels present |
| `plddt_occluded_probs` | float | probability with the pLDDT channel pair occluded |
| `rsa_occluded_probs` | float | probability with the RSA channel pair occluded |
| `helix_occluded_probs` | float | probability with helix channels 4–6 occluded |
| `sheet_occluded_probs` | float | probability with sheet channels 7–8 occluded |
| `coil_occluded_probs` | float | probability with coil channels 9–11 occluded |

One methodological caveat for advanced readers: the repository ships the *results* of the intervention, not the intervention script itself. The exact replacement convention applied to the masked channels (e.g., zeroing versus mean-substitution) is not encoded in any shipped file; only the downstream consumers and their CSV inputs are in the tree. When extending the corpus, any re-implementation should preserve the schema above, since both figure scripts parse it positionally.

Sources: [reproduction/README.md](reproduction/README.md#L1-L24), [DP03818_occlusion.csv](reproduction/results/occlusion_analysis/DP03818_occlusion.csv#L1-L2), [caid3_binding.fasta](data/test/caid3_binding.fasta#L1-L4), [data/README.md](data/README.md#L24-L27), [figure_4.py](reproduction/scripts/figure_4.py#L9-L35)

> [!TIP]
> Before reusing these CSVs in your own analyses, verify row alignment against the FASTA: `DP03818_occlusion.csv` rows map 1:1 to `caid3_binding.fasta`'s sequence line and its `1111111111111` label line. This residue/label correspondence check is the fastest way to catch corpus or schema drift when new proteins are added.

## Figure 3: Global Importance via ROC Degradation and ΔAUC

`figure_3.py` answers the dataset-wide question: *if a feature group is removed, how much binding discrimination does the model lose?* The pipeline pools every residue from all 51 files, then treats each probability column (original plus five occluded variants) as an independent score against the shared `y` labels:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["51 files in<br/>reproduction/results/occlusion_analysis/"] --> B["read_occlusion_result_file()<br/>parse residue, y, 6 probability columns"]
    B --> C["pool residues across proteins<br/>extend shared lists per key"]
    C --> D["ROC curve per score column<br/>(original + 5 occluded)"]
    D --> E["AUC per variant"]
    E --> F["delta AUC = AUC_original − AUC_occluded<br/>per feature group"]
```

The script prints the original AUC alongside each occluded AUC and its delta (`original_auc - auc`), so the group with the largest ΔAUC is the one whose removal most damages discrimination over the whole corpus. Overlaid ROC curves additionally show *where* along the FPR/TPR trade-off each occlusion hurts — a pair of channels (pLDDT, RSA) versus the three- or two-channel SS3-derived groups can be compared on identical residue sets because the `y` labels never change across variants.

Sources: [figure_3.py](reproduction/scripts/figure_3.py#L9-L35), [figure_3.py](reproduction/scripts/figure_3.py#L38-L47), [figure_3.py](reproduction/scripts/figure_3.py#L71-L88)

## Figure 4: Per-Residue Delta Probabilities Stratified by Prediction Outcome

`figure_4.py` complements Figure 3 with a local, signed quantity. For every residue and every group it computes the delta probability `Δp = original_probs − <group>_occluded_probs`:

- **Δp > 0** — occluding the group *lowered* the score: the feature argued for binding at that residue.
- **Δp ≈ 0** — the group was unused at that residue.
- **Δp < 0** — occluding the group *raised* the score: the feature argued against binding there.

Distributions of Δp per group are drawn as violin plots (with per-group means marked by stars), first over the full corpus and then stratified by the confusion-matrix class of the baseline prediction using the production decision threshold of **0.26** — the same threshold baked into `daruma_binding` because it maximizes F1 on validation data:

| Stratum | Mask condition | Analytical question answered |
|---|---|---|
| True Positive (4b) | `y == 1` and `p ≥ 0.26` | which features *sustain* correctly detected binding sites |
| False Negative (4c) | `y == 1` and `p < 0.26` | which missing feature evidence let true sites slip through |
| False Positive (4d) | `y == 0` and `p ≥ 0.26` | which features *drove* the false alarms |
| True Negative (4e) | `y == 0` and `p < 0.26` | which features keep non-binding residues suppressed |

Comparing the four strata turns raw feature importance into error diagnosis — for example, a feature group with large positive Δp among false negatives indicates a structural cue the model fails to exploit where it matters most, while large positive Δp among false positives pinpoints the evidence responsible for over-prediction. This strata view is the per-residue counterpart to the global ΔAUC: Figure 3 ranks the groups in aggregate, Figure 4 explains *whose* predictions each group moves, and in which direction.

Sources: [figure_4.py](reproduction/scripts/figure_4.py#L80-L86), [figure_4.py](reproduction/scripts/figure_4.py#L38-L53), [figure_4.py](reproduction/scripts/figure_4.py#L99-L104), [figure_4.py](reproduction/scripts/figure_4.py#L106-L153), [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L199)

## The Two-Lens Design: Comparing the Analyses

The two figure scripts form a deliberate attribution pipeline over the same artifacts — understanding their division of labor helps when interpreting or extending the results:

| Aspect | Figure 3 (`figure_3.py`) | Figure 4 (`figure_4.py`) |
|---|---|---|
| Signal analyzed | raw probabilities (original vs. each occluded variant) | signed delta `Δp = original − occluded` |
| Aggregation | dataset-wide ROC/AUC over pooled residues | per-residue distributions, split by confusion stratum |
| Primary output | ranking of feature groups by ΔAUC | shape/mean of Δp per group per TP/FN/FP/TN class |
| Question | which group, when removed, most degrades discrimination? | how does each group shift individual scores, for which outcomes? |

Sources: [figure_3.py](reproduction/scripts/figure_3.py#L71-L88), [figure_4.py](reproduction/scripts/figure_4.py#L80-L86)

## What the Analysis Establishes — and Its Limits

Read together, the two analyses attribute the binding head's behavior entirely to five predicted structural signals, because no other information path exists between the ProtT5 embedding and the binding decision. Positive delta mass concentrated in specific groups reveals which structural concepts the binding head has learned to exploit; negative deltas expose evidence the head actively discounts. Three limitations should frame any interpretation. First, attribution is at feature-group granularity — the paired softmax channels and SS3-derived sums cannot be decomposed further without re-running the intervention at single-channel resolution. Second, the artifacts were generated against the CAID3 binding test distribution; Δp magnitudes are not guaranteed to transfer to other protein classes. Third, as noted above, the masking convention lives outside the shipped code, so exact reproduction of the CSVs requires the manuscript's protocol rather than this repository alone.

Sources: [models.py](src/daruma_binding/backend/models.py#L157-L188), [reproduction/README.md](reproduction/README.md#L1-L24), [figure_4.py](reproduction/scripts/figure_4.py#L106-L153)
